👋 Hey there!
If you need a *report*, please refer to FleetX (DriverX). If your request concerns an *invoice*, follow these steps:

1. Open the **Client page in Admin**: [link|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/billing-rides/clients?tz=Europe%2FTallinn&filter=%7B%22limit%22%3A25%2C%22offset%22%3A0%2C%22filter%22%3A%7B%7D%7D].
2. Enter the Fleet or Driver ID in the **External ID** filter field.
3. Open the driver or fleet profile.
4. Go to the **Invoice tasks** tab.
   * If you see *Invoice sum too small*, no commission invoice was generated because the driver either owed no commission or had more compensation than commission.
   * If you encounter any other error, please let us know.
5. Commission invoices for the entire history of the fleet/driver are available either under **Invoice tasks** or **Partner Invoices**.

Best regards,
*Billing Ops AI*

Added a simple alert to check day over day for active benefits to subscriptions alerting:

{noformat}select 
    smo.id as offer_id,
    concat('https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/campaign-subscriptions/offers/demand/', cast(smo.id as varchar(255))) as provider_url,
    sbb.type as benefit_type,
    count(sbtbu.id) as usage_count
from ng_public_spark.subscription_marketplace_offer smo
join ng_public_spark.subscription_benefits_benefit sbb on
    sbb.offer_id = smo.id 
    and sbb.state = 'approved'
    and sbb.type in (
        'free_cancellation',
        'ride_cashback', 
        'rental_free_unlock', 
        'free_delivery', 
        'delivery_service_fee_discount'
    )
left join ng_public_spark.subscription_benefits_target_benefit_usage sbtbu on
    sbtbu.benefit_id = sbb.id
    and sbtbu.created >= DATE(NOW()) - INTERVAL 1 DAY
    and sbtbu.created <= NOW()
where
    smo.state = 'approved'
    and smo.id not in (
        5, -- Berlin offer for Jina
        52, -- Old offer in Croatia
        50 -- Old offer in Norway
    )
group by
    smo.id, 
    sbb.type 
having
    count(sbtbu.id) = 0
;{noformat}

Advise the customer to *check with their bank* to confirm the release of the preauthorisation. Banks handle these releases differently, and while some are immediate, others may process it as a temporary charge that is then refunded. Sometimes, the payment is reversed without the bank sending a reversal notification to the customer, which might lead the user to think that the reversal has not been made.

The reversal can take up to *30 days* to complete, as pending authorisations typically expire after that time on banks end.

Unfortunately, we don't have full visibility into all the parties involved in the payment processing beyond our payment partner. Therefore, we can't track the exact status of the preauthorisation release once it has been sent.

Thank you,

Marten

Clause 1 (Purpose) 
Could we put focus on the provision of services instead of renting the equipment? This would help us to argue that Bolt is paying for a service and that the kiosks are incidental part to it, and should not be a permanent establishment of Bolt abroad.

Clause 3 (Scope and Term)
Same remark as clause 1

Clause 3.2.
The narrative of Bolt as intermediary is not applicable for tax purposes in the case of resale model, as in this case Bolt is deemed to have, for tax matters, bought and resold the service. This is the known different view between tax and legal on resale model.

Clause 3.3. Absent in the contract, it goes from 3.2 to 3.4.

Clause 6.2. Technology Fee
Naming the clause as such increases the risk that payments will be treated as royalties, so a withholding tax would be applicable to it (which could increase the cost of Bolt to get the software). Is there a way in which payment is structured as a payment for services, which include hardware, provision of services, management, etc.?

Clause 6.4. Taxes
It is stated that Kiosk provider will bear the cost of withholding taxes. When we presented this to kiosk providers we were told that they could not accept this clause, that their payments should be net. Did they end up agreeing to this?

Advise the customer to *check with their bank* to confirm the release of the preauthorisation. Banks handle these releases differently, and while some are immediate, others may process it as a temporary charge that is then refunded. Sometimes, the payment is reversed without the bank sending a reversal notification to the customer, which might lead the user to think that the reversal has not been made.

The reversal can take up to *30 days* to complete, as pending authorisations typically expire after that time on banks end.

Unfortunately, we don't have full visibility into all the parties involved in the payment processing beyond our payment partner. Therefore, we can't track the exact status of the preauthorisation release once it has been sent.

Thank you,

Marten

Hi [~accountid:5d15dd8c0d64020c403ae98c] and [~accountid:712020:dbc22d70-1983-4414-80b3-27f087787ae4] , thanks a lot! 🙏 

I am aligned with [~accountid:712020:dbc22d70-1983-4414-80b3-27f087787ae4] - from a legal POV, the address relates to a legal person and as such, is not personal data in this context. That said, I understand that it _also_ relates to the data subject in his personal capacity. However, as [~accountid:712020:dbc22d70-1983-4414-80b3-27f087787ae4] highlights - under French accounting and tax law, invoices must include the service provider’s identifying details, including the company address. Here, the invoice is issued in the name of the driver’s company, not the driver as a private individual. In that context, the address qualifies as a professional identifier. Even if the company address coincides with the driver’s home address, the processing is still lawful, as the GDPR does not override statutory invoicing obligations. Our legal basis for processing the data is compliance with a legal obligation under Article 6(1)(c) GDPR, and data subject rights like erasure or objection do not apply where processing is mandatory by law.

*What we can realistically communicate to the drivers here:*

* Explain clearly that Bolt is legally required to display the company address on invoices in France.
* Suggest, if the driver wants to avoid this going forward, that they register a separate professional address if legally permissible for their business.

Please follow the steps in this Knowledge Base article to advise the customer: [https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/kb/articles/internal/7109163016850?country=global&language=en|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/kb/articles/internal/7109163016850?country=global&language=en]

Advise the customer to *check with their bank* to confirm the release of the preauthorisation. Banks handle these releases differently, and while some are immediate, others may process it as a temporary charge that is then refunded. Sometimes, the payment is reversed without the bank sending a reversal notification to the customer, which might lead the user to think that the reversal has not been made.

The reversal can take up to *30 days* to complete, as pending authorisations typically expire after that time on banks end.

Unfortunately, we don't have full visibility into all the parties involved in the payment processing beyond our payment partner. Therefore, we can't track the exact status of the preauthorisation release once it has been sent.

Thank you,

Marten

Hi [~accountid:712020:88708e1d-c334-4279-9692-ef3f2432966b] I’ve reviewed the document against the PWD and Bolt’s internal [PWD privacy position|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1iQ1jZrrbeIKDK98hdHQTO5q6bQ-6B16lsq5UneOFq-4/edit?tab=t.0#heading=h.9dfsqojnamqt]. Overall, the document broadly reflects the direction of the PWD, but in several places it goes further than what the PWD strictly requires and would create unnecessary legal and operational exposure for Bolt if accepted as-is.

* the doc effectively assumes that all relevant platform processes qualify as automated monitoring or automated decision-making. While the PWD does define digital labour platforms by reference to automated systems, it still relies on factual assessment of how systems actually operate. Treating all processes as ADM by default removes needed flexibility and risks over-triggering obligations that should only apply where legal thresholds are met.
* the DPIA section is too expansive. The PWD requires DPIAs for automated monitoring and decision-making systems because they are considered high risk, but it does not justify extending DPIA requirements to non-automated or low-risk processing. The doc should be narrowed to clearly link DPIAs only to qualifying automated systems, otherwise we risk creating GDPR obligations that do not exist.
** Related to this, the document overreaches on DPIA disclosure. Seeking views of workers and sharing the DPIA with representatives is required, but broader or automatic disclosure to authorities or other parties without a specific request goes beyond the PWD and raises confidentiality and security concerns.
* On data portability, the document correctly reflects that platform workers have enhanced portability rights for data generated through platform work, such as ratings and reviews. However, this should be framed as a platform-specific right and aligned with GDPR mechanics. Any attempt to introduce separate formats, tooling, or timelines beyond what is necessary would add avoidable engineering and compliance complexity.
* he transparency provisions are largely in line with the PWD, but the document risks becoming too prescriptive in practice. The Directive requires +*meaningful*+ information about data categories, parameters, and decision impacts, not disclosure of algorithmic logic, source code, or commercially sensitive details. Any interpretation that pushes toward that level of disclosure is not acceptable and would undermine Bolt’s freedom to conduct its business.
* The human oversight and human decision-making requirements are mandatory under the PWD for decisions with adverse or equivalent effects, such as account restriction or termination. However, +*the document should not be read as requiring human involvement for every operational or low-impact decision*+. Extending human review beyond clearly detrimental decisions would exceed the Directive and be disproportionate.
* it does not sufficiently reflect the proportionality principle. The PWD explicitly expects Member States to avoid unnecessary administrative, legal, and financial burdens. Additional reporting, consultation, or documentation layers that are not clearly required by the Directive should be resisted, particularly where they would fragment processes across markets or undermine scalability.

h3. ✅ What can be shared (high-level, non-personal, non-committal)

We may respond *at a very high level*, for example:

* Confirm that:
** Bolt takes safety complaints seriously

** Appropriate measures are taken in line with Bolt policies and applicable law

This should be *generic and policy-level*, not case-specific.

h3. ❌ What should NOT be shared

We should *not disclose*:

* Whether the driver was suspended, blocked, or disciplined
* Results or status of any internal investigation
* Whether compensation was considered or offered
* Details of safety reviews, checks, or internal escalations
* Any internal documents or correspondence

As in the previous case, we should:

* Clearly state that:
** Detailed information and documents can only be disclosed *to competent law enforcement authorities or pursuant to a court order*
** Bolt is willing to cooperate fully with such authorities

Update - done regarding:

* detail of {{consult_with_supervisor}} breakdown based on month experience

* Top 10 issue key breakdowns

Key Learning:

* In a multi-pod setup, *Next.js in-memory caching is per pod*, not shared.
* {{unstable_cache}} only caches within a single pod, so requests routed to different pods cause duplicate API calls.
* *React’s* {{cache()}} only deduplicates within one render execution and does not work across HTTP requests or separate contexts like {{generateMetadata}}, page renders, and OpenGraph routes.
* A single page load can trigger *multiple concurrent server requests* (metadata, page, OG image), which may hit different pods.
* *Real solution:* use a *shared cache (Redis/Memcached)*. Without it, duplicate API calls are unavoidable in horizontally scaled Next.js deployments.

After initial request and pods having cache memory we dont see same request in kibana being logged so unstable cache is indeed working.

We did make some good to do changes which reduced some calls
1. Include position_id in cache key
2. Return null instead of notFound()  because notFound() is not cached by next js

Advise the customer to *check with their bank* to confirm the release of the preauthorisation. Banks handle these releases differently, and while some are immediate, others may process it as a temporary charge that is then refunded. Sometimes, the payment is reversed without the bank sending a reversal notification to the customer, which might lead the user to think that the reversal has not been made.

The reversal can take up to *30 days* to complete, as pending authorisations typically expire after that time on banks end.

Unfortunately, we don't have full visibility into all the parties involved in the payment processing beyond our payment partner. Therefore, we can't track the exact status of the preauthorisation release once it has been sent.

{code:sql}WITH to_from_rules AS (

Bolt Group rate is very low as compare to approved rates by US government so this is not possible. As per the response from local accounting partner, one fixed rate is not possible. There is an option like high-low approach which means, we can set one fixed rate with the low cost locations and one for high cost locations but again we need to create two rates for each type of per diem (Domestic and International). Please see below the response. 

Per Diem for International Travel (e.g., Tallinn, Estonia)

As noted earlier, there is no single global per diem standard, and organizations typically either (i) set per diem rates by country or city or (ii) adopt a simplified structure such as a high–low approach. Rates can be found here: [https://allowances.state.gov/web920/per_diem.asp?|https://allowances.state.gov/web920/per_diem.asp?|smart-link] 

From a practical standpoint, many employers do *not* provide a single upfront “daily allowance” covering all travel costs, as this can exceed actual expenses. Instead, they commonly operate under an accountable plan, where lodging and transportation are reimbursed based on actual costs with receipts, and meals & incidental expenses (M&IE) may be reimbursed using a per diem rate for administrative simplicity.

For the upcoming travel to Tallinn, Estonia, a reasonable per diem benchmark—based on commonly used international government travel guidance—would be:

* Lodging: USD 217 per night
* Meals & Incidentals (M&IE): USD 139 per day
* Total Daily Per Diem: USD 356

For U.S. domestic travel, the standard federal per diem (for most locations) is currently:

* Lodging: USD 107 per night
* Meals & Incidentals (M&IE): USD 59 per day
* Total Standard Per Diem: USD 166 per day

Some higher-cost cities (for example, New York, San Francisco, Washington, D.C., etc.) have higher per diem limits. These are published by the U.S. General Services Administration and vary by city and by time of year.

Regards,

Deepak

** On the same day, the rider claimed that their email address was wrong and that someone had changed their phone number.
*** The phone number that the rider complained about has been on the account since 2024 (and it was changed on 15 December 2025). The same goes for the email address. This suggests that the contact information on the account was correct, but the complainant does not recognise it (i.e., they are the new user).
*** The original name on the account with Ali Hassan. On 30 September, it was changed to Felipe Rocha (this is the name of the complainant). This mirrors a new login from the original phone number (ending in 6608) on 29 September 2025. All new logins in December have been from the new phone number (ending in 5093).
** On 14 December, CS connected all devices from the account.
*** Rider still insists on a refund.
**** Payment method for the trip at-issue was made using a card added in Nov 2025 (ending in 1177). This is Felipe’s, as Ali has separately confirmed that their card is the one ending in 7574.
*** CS then seemingly sat on this. After a while, on 24 December, the rider wrote back again ([here|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/case/710781078]), frustrated. They are threatening to escalate to the authorities.
* NB. Separately, in November 2025, Ali messaged CS via the same account ([here|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/case/684360728]) saying “_i was using thi account from last 3 years.but unfortunately i miss my number last year and now someone has same number and using my bolt into his name but problem is he used my email and my bank account can you please remove my account or block this account i will be very thankful to you_”. This was not escalated to Privacy Team.
** This confirms that this is a case of phone number recycling.

+*ANALYSIS*+

* We can be confident that the account is compromised (most likely phone number recycling).
** It appears that Ali first set up the account, and then Felipe likely gained access in September 2025 through recycling of the phone number ending in 6608. Ali continued to have access during that time, and so took trips on the account, which Felipe eventually noticed and complained about. Felipe has now changed the account details to their, and CS has logged out all devices, which likely now includes Ali. As such, it seems Felipe has access to Ali’s account.
** I have reported this to the ODPO Team [here|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C0678KJ49UH/p1767022930476689]. This seems unlikely to be reportable.
* This incident is currently ongoing, and so we will need to archive the account / recommend that Felipe set up a new account (and inform Ali of the same).

* Ensure that the account is archived, and messages are sent to both Felipe and Ali (via email).

After taking a closer look at the legal act, I can confirm that it matches what the team previously outlined.

In essence:

From *1 January 2026*, Lithuania will introduce a *10% “security contribution” fee* on *non-life insurance* policies that are *concluded, renewed/extended, or amended* on or after that date.

No fee will apply to policies that were *signed and paid before 1 January 2026*, as long as they are *not amended* after that date.

The fee will be *included in the total amount payable* by the customer.

The collected funds are *not insurance company revenue*: they will be *transferred to the State Defence Fund* to finance national defence and security spending—meaning individuals and businesses contribute directly to strengthening the country’s defence.

*Exceptions (when the fee will not apply):*
The law provides an exemption for *mandatory motor third-party liability insurance* only where the vehicle is used *exclusively for personal purposes* and *not in economic activity*.

Therefore, *drivers providing RH services* (i.e., using the vehicle for economic activity) will *fall within the scope of this fee*, and the *10% security contribution will apply to them from the New Year (1 January 2026)*.

If you have any additional questions, please let me know, thanks!

Hi Team,

Advise the customer to *check with their bank* to confirm the release of the preauthorisation. Banks handle these releases differently, and while some are immediate, others may process it as a temporary charge that is then refunded. Sometimes, the payment is reversed without the bank sending a reversal notification to the customer, which might lead the user to think that the reversal has not been made.

The reversal can take up to *30 days* to complete, as pending authorisations typically expire after that time on banks end.

Unfortunately, we don't have full visibility into all the parties involved in the payment processing beyond our payment partner. Therefore, we can't track the exact status of the preauthorisation release once it has been sent.

Thank you,

Marten

Sometimes, the payment is reversed without the bank sending a reversal notification to the customer, which might lead the user to think that the reversal has not been made.

The reversal can take up to *30 days* to complete, as pending authorisations typically expire after that time on banks end.

Unfortunately, we don't have full visibility into all the parties involved in the payment processing beyond our payment partner. Therefore, we can't track the exact status of the preauthorisation release once it has been sent.

Thank you,

Marten

This means that you are responsible for ensuring that any recording or sharing of passenger data complies with the GDPR and local legislation, particularly regarding transparency, consent, and lawful processing.

However, you remain accountable for ensuring compliance with data protection law and for any breaches arising from your or your drivers’ actions.

Hello,

Thank you for the response from your legal department.

I acknowledge your reference to the Data Sharing Agreement and the assertion that delivery partners act as independent data controllers. However, this position does not resolve the legal deficiencies present in this case.

Even where delivery partners qualify as independent data controllers, Bolt remains obligated under GDPR to ensure that personal data is shared and processed within a framework that guarantees appropriate technical and organisational safeguards. This responsibility cannot be discharged solely through contractual terms if those safeguards are demonstrably ineffective in practice.

You have confirmed that the courier failed to use Bolt’s official communication channel and instead contacted me from a private number via WhatsApp. This constitutes a clear breakdown of the safeguards Bolt claims to rely upon. Under Articles 5(2) and 24 GDPR, Bolt must not only establish compliance measures but must also be able to demonstrate their effective implementation. The admitted deviation shows that such implementation failed in this instance.

Furthermore, the classification of delivery partners as independent data controllers does not negate Bolt’s obligations under the principles of transparency, fairness, and integrity of processing under Article 5(1)(a) and 5(1)(f) GDPR. From the data subject’s perspective, being contacted through an unofficial private channel falls outside any reasonable expectation of how personal data will be processed when using Bolt’s platform.

Additionally, your statement that Bolt is “not in a position to fully control how individual couriers use the phone number” raises a serious compliance concern. If Bolt cannot ensure adherence to its own prescribed safeguards, this directly calls into question whether the data-sharing arrangement itself meets GDPR requirements for lawful, secure, and accountable processing.

While you conclude that no personal data breach occurred, GDPR does not require malicious intent or third-party disclosure for an infringement to exist. The unauthorized use of personal data outside established and communicated safeguards constitutes improper processing, regardless of purpose limitation.

In light of the above, I do not accept your conclusion that this matter falls outside GDPR liability. I will therefore consider submitting a formal complaint to the competent data protection authority for independent assessment of Bolt’s compliance with Articles 5, 24, and 32 GDPR.

Please confirm that this correspondence is retained as part of your GDPR compliance documentation.

Kind regards, Lazarus

+*BACKGROUND*+

* On 12 December, Arundeep Sandhu (UK Ops) sent an email to 29 Bolt drivers which congratulated them for completing their first trip by sending them a £5.00 Costa gift card. Unfortunately, Arundeep sent all of the gift cards in the same bulk email (rather than individually). As a result: (i) each recipient could see the email address of the other 28 drivers; and (ii) any recipient could redeem all of the gift cards themselves.
** Based on team discussions on Slack ([link|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/CGXCR7ML4/p1767092523459849?thread_ts=1767083075.197529&cid=CGXCR7ML4]), the emails should have been sent individually. As such, this is an example of human error.
* On 29 December, one of the 29 recipients ([Mesut Yuce|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/fleet/drivers/edit/8292168?tab=profile&filter=%7B%22limit%22%3A25%2C%22offset%22%3A0%2C%22filter%22%3A%7B%7D%7D&tz=Europe%2FTallinn]) emailed Bolt ([link|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/case/713555021]) claiming that this is “_a serious breach of Data Protection laws_”. The driver demands an immediate investigation into this, and are threatening legal action if nothing is done.
** The driver has also complained that all of the gift cards were used / nominal by the time he tried to redeem them. As such, the driver also wants compensation.

+*ANALYSIS*+

* This is a confirmed personal data breach. As such, this has been escalated to the ODPO Team [+*here*+|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C0678KJ49UH/p1767101170097129]. It is unlikely to be reportable.
** The breached data is the email address of each driver.
** No financial detriment has been suffered per se - The drivers did not previously own the gift cards.
* In terms of mitigation steps, all that we can do (since the email has already been sent) is: (i) ask each recipient to delete the email; and (ii) considering re-sending individual gift cards (to prevent driver complaints).
** NB. The issue of the used/nominal gift cards (and whether to re-issue them) is not an issue for the Privacy Team, and should be handled by Ops. However, this would lower the risk of any of the drivers complaining, and so it would be the preferred approach.
* NB. We are currently only aware of this email, but it is worth checking for completeness that no others have been sent (this is unlikely, as it appears to be a one-off mistake).

+*NEXT STEPS*+

* QUESTIONS:
** Was only one bulk email sent, or are there other examples?
** Have any of the other drivers complained?
* RESOLUTION:
** (1) Await ODPO findings re data breach report.
** (2) Discuss options with Ops regarding re-sending the gift cards.
** (3) Send an email to each of the recipients apologising for the incident and asking them to delete the email from their inbox (and flagging what is being done about the gift cards).

Advise the customer to *check with their bank* to confirm the release of the preauthorisation. Banks handle these releases differently, and while some are immediate, others may process it as a temporary charge that is then refunded. Sometimes, the payment is reversed without the bank sending a reversal notification to the customer, which might lead the user to think that the reversal has not been made.

The reversal can take up to *30 days* to complete, as pending authorisations typically expire after that time on banks end.

Unfortunately, we don't have full visibility into all the parties involved in the payment processing beyond our payment partner. Therefore, we can't track the exact status of the preauthorisation release once it has been sent.

[~accountid:61b8c1da9e8a370068a18370] Legally speaking, as explained in our [Photo Scraping Guidance|https://taxify.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/LEG/pages/4854710327/Photo+scraping], scraping product photos and displaying them involves:

* reproduction (copying the image); and
* communication to the public (making it available on our platform).

*Both acts generally require the permission of the relevant copyright holder (NB! Do not assume that merchants own the rights).*

Product photos on packaging or on manufacturer websites are normally protected by copyright. The fact that a photo has a “commercial” or “standard” look (for example, a photo of a Coca-Cola can) does not exclude copyright protection.

Copyright protection may be excluded in limited cases, mainly where a photo is found to lack originality. However, originality is assessed on a case-by-case basis, typically in the context of a dispute. In practice, Bolt would need to argue and substantiate that a particular photo is not original, which is very difficult. Photos on product packaging usually meet the originality threshold, even if they appear “commercial” or “standard”, because the photographer can rely on creative choices such as lighting, composition, angle, or post-processing. EU case law confirms this approach.

Accordingly, we must assume that rights exist, and therefore *photo scraping presents a high legal risk*.

Cooperation with merchants or manufacturers does not grant Bolt any automatic right to use product photos. *Third-party product photos may only be used where Bolt has a contractual licence or where the merchant has provided the photos (uploaded or provided a download link) and warranted the necessary rights* (typically through acceptance of our T&Cs)*.* However, if a merchant provides photos without holding the required rights, such warranties do not eliminate Bolt’s liability towards copyright holders. They only provide a basis for seeking compensation from the merchant for damages resulting from third-party claims.

When storing and using images in the catalog, PIM, or store menus, the instructions in the [Menu Scraping Guidelines|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1OTsT8j8dyuurGsw1eoCKPWSwHl219rFFMjjEBM4BurU/edit?usp=sharing] must be followed. In particular, photos must not be scraped from competitors’ webpages. A clear retention and deletion policy must also be defined, including time limits and deletion triggers (e.g. periodic deletion or termination of cooperation with the relevant brand or merchant).

After upgrading Elementary from 0.14.1 to 0.20, {{dbt_invocations}} and {{dbt_run_results}} stopped being populated for dbt runs on Databricks job clusters. The {{on-run-end}} hook was reported as successful, but no SQL was executed after the models finished, so the upload effectively became a silent no-op.

Between {{0.14}} and {{0.20}}, a new guard ({{is_elementary_enabled}}) was added. This guard checks whether Elementary can resolve the database and schema where its models live. With the {{dbt-spark}} adapter, {{target.database}} is always {{NULL}}, so Elementary concluded it was disabled and exited early. With {{dbt-databricks}}, {{target.database}} is correctly set to {{hive_metastore}}, which is why the same setup worked in CI and Airflow (we’re still using {{dbt-databricks}} there).

To mitigate this issue, we can add a Spark-specific override for Elementary’s {{get_package_database_and_schema}}. For Spark targets, if the database is missing, I default it to {{hive_metastore}} (configurable via a var). We’ll need to add a dispatch rule in each root project so Elementary resolves this override from the common package. This makes {{is_elementary_enabled}} evaluate to true again and restores invocation and run-result uploads on job clusters.

This relates to the wider problem that in {{dbt-spark}} there’s no notion of {{database}} / {{catalog}} - which can become a problem once we have to switch to the Unity Catalog.

Hi team, 

That’s a great question! Thanks for showing interest in this topic! 

Visa / Mastercard Account Updater is a network service that automatically keeps stored card details (Card-on-File) up to date when a cardholder’s card changes. This is done through the cards network token. 

When a customer’s card is *replaced or updated*, the card networks like Visa or MasterCard can provide Bolt with:

* New *card number*
* Updated *expiry date*
* In some cases, an updated *card status* (active / closed)

This is useful for the customer for multiple different services without having to manually update their own card details and avoid service interruptions. However, understandably sometimes this can cause confusion. 

* Subscriptions
* Recurring billing
* Merchant-Initiated Transactions (MITs)
* Ride-hailing, food delivery, streaming, utilities

Hope this answers your question! 

Cheers, 
Marten

I’ve reviewed the GitHub [Data Protection Agreement|https://github.com/customer-terms/github-data-protection-agreement] and, from a contractual standpoint, GitHub is an approved vendor for processing personal data on Bolt’s behalf. The agreement includes the relevant transfer safeguards (including SCCs), so there is no contractual blocker to using GitHub Actions as such (/) 

But there are a few practical risk considerations worth keeping in mind for this specific use case.

GitHub Actions runners are part of CI infrastructure and, even though GitHub does not access the data intentionally, personal data processed can end up in logs/other outputs. This increases exposure in case of misconfiguration or leakage and is generally harder to control than processing inside internal systems.

For prompt evaluation, it seems like raw personal data is not actually needed to achieve the goal. Because of that, using unmasked support chat data is simply less defensible and creates avoidable risk if something goes wrong.

From a privacy perspective, my recommendation is:

* If possible, filter or mask personal data in the evaluation datasets before running them in GitHub Actions.
* Keep any data used in CI jobs short-lived and clean it up or overwrite it as soon as the job finishes.

I’ve completed a privacy assessment and, overall, the setup is fine to proceed. Masking or reducing personal data in the datasets would materially lower risk and is strongly encouraged, but we’re not asking you to stop work if that can be done in parallel.

If we can’t mask the data or reduce the amount of personal data in this project - let me know (esp. why we can’t do it) and I’ll make sure to include this in my assessment 🙏

Hi [~accountid:712020:9b23c511-5079-4424-a07c-0f962904588e] did the driver activate “Fare Review” feature in the app within the prescribed deadline? If not then we can send him the following response. 

Poštovani, 

ovim putem odgovaramo na Vaš *službeni prigovor* u vezi s vožnjom od 27. prosinca 2025. u 01:10 h, na relaciji Školska – Čička, u kojoj je putnik, prema Vašim navodima, napustio vozilo bez plaćanja gotovinom. Uz prigovor ste istaknuli zahtjev za:

# Potpuno storniranje vožnje,
# Poništavanje i povrat zaračunate Bolt provizije i PDV-a na istu,
# Pismeno obrazloženje pravne osnove obračuna provizije za nenaplaćeni iznos.

U nastavku dostavljamo očitovanje.

1. *Pravni i ugovorni okvir*

Vaš odnos s platformom Bolt uređuje se *Općim uvjetima za vozače* , koji čine važeći ugovor između Vas, kao pružatelja usluge prijevoza, i društva Bolt Operations OÜ, kao posrednika u organizaciji usluge putem digitalne platforme.

Bolt, kao digitalna usluga informacijskog društva, e pruža uslugu prijevoza vec djeluje isključivo kao posrednik između neovisnog pružatelja usluge (Vozača) i krajnjeg korisnika (Putnika) i nije ugovorna strana u usluzi prijevoza, sukladno članku 10.1 Općih uvjeta. 

U skladu s time, prema članku 4.10 Općih uvjeta , u slučajevima kada je odabrana opcija gotovinskog plaćanja, isključiva odgovornost za naplatu leži na vozaču. Ako putnik odbije platiti, Bolt može poslati obavijest o dugu putniku u Vaše ime, no to ne stvara obvezu Bolta da nadoknadi iznos ili stornira vožnju.

_“U slučaju da Putnik plaća Naknadu za vožnju izravno Vama, Vaša je obveza izvršiti naplatu. Ako Putnik odbije platiti, Bolt će, u Vaše ime, poslati obavijest o dugu Putniku. Takva ovlast ne znači da je Bolt obvezan nadoknaditi Naknadu za vožnju.”_

2. *Institucija “Fare Review” – funkcionalna i pravna svrha*

Za situacije u kojima vozač smatra da je izračunata cijena netočna, da vožnja nije izvedena do kraja ili da nije naplaćena, ugovorom je predviđena procedura putem aplikacije, nazvana *“Fare Review”*.

Prema *članku 4.8*, vozač je dužan:

_“...podnijeti zahtjev u odjeljku ‘Fare Review’ unutar aplikacije. Ako zahtjev nije podnesen tim putem, Bolt neće izvršiti ponovni obračun ili nadoknadu.”_

Taj zahtjev se mora podnijeti *isključivo unutar aplikacije i u zadanom vremenskom roku*, neposredno nakon završetka vožnje. Naš tim tada ima pristup svim relevantnim tehničkim podacima (npr. GPS putanja, trajanje, status putnika) i temeljem toga može:

* umanjiti ili stornirati iznos,
* ukloniti proviziju,
* ili potvrditi postojeći iznos ako vožnja prema sustavu rezultira kao izvršena.

Ako zahtjev nije podnesen unutar aplikacije putem funkcije „Fare Review“, Bolt ne može naknadno intervenirati, što je jasno definirano Uvjetima. Žalbe podnesene putem e-maila, chata ili drugih kanala, nažalost, ne zamjenjuju pravodobno korištenje te funkcije.

3. *Naplaćena Bolt naknada – pravna osnova*

Naplaćena Bolt provizija temelji se na uspješno dovršenim vožnjama prema aplikaciji, sukladno *članku 5.1*:

_“Vozač je dužan platiti Bolt Fee za svaku izvršenu narudžbu usluge prijevoza. Visina Bolt Fee-a i poreza prikazuje se u aplikaciji ili u partner portalu.”_

S obzirom na to da vožnja nije označena kao neuspješna u sustavu, ista se smatrala *uredno dovršenom*, a provizija obračunata u skladu s uvjetima. Ispravak je moguć samo ako se koristi dostupna funkcija „Fare Review“ i ako su tehnički podaci u sustavu u skladu s navodima vozača.

4. *Napomena o poreznom aspektu*

Razumijemo da ste kao porezni obveznik dužni prijaviti sve transakcije, uključujući i nenaplaćene, ako su iskazane u fakturi. Međutim, Bolt ne može utjecati na porezne prijave vozača, niti odgovara za poreznu obvezu temeljem propisa o fiskalizaciji. U skladu s *člankom 4.15*, odgovornost za poreznu i računovodstvenu obradu prihoda isključivo snosi pružatelj usluge.

5. *Zaključno*

Vaš zahtjev za storniranje vožnje i povrat naknada ne ispunjava formalne i sadržajne uvjete za odobrenje, jer:

* naplata nije izvršena, ali nije zabilježena kroz sustav „Fare Review“;
* sustav je vožnju registrirao kao završenu i nije prijavljen tehnički kvar ni odstupanje;
* nije utvrđeno kršenje uvjeta od strane Bolta.

Zahvaljujemo na razumijevanju i dostupni smo za dodatna pojašnjenja ili pravnu dokumentaciju koju eventualno zatražite.

S poštovanjem,
*Bolt Operations OÜ*

So far, we’ve been receiving images directly from our partners, and we’ve been reusing them across our platform to cover products that don’t have images. Until now, I was under the impression — based on previous guidance — that we are allowed to keep and freely reuse these images across all partner menus.

That’s why I’d like to better understand how we should handle image usage rights and potential “time limits” for content received from partners or image providers such as BrandBank.

First and foremost, we should ensure that we have explicit [consent|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1HLQ4cUo8GIgotOsErnBK54btQc2746HOMbgdFiANM2s/template/preview] from each partner to use the images they provide. We currently reuse those images across other partners when needed. However, if there are limitations on how long we can store or reuse these images, or if we’re required to remove them when a partner leaves the platform, it could pose a challenge. Basically, removing those images would also remove them from any other partners where they were reused, leading to significant gaps in product assortment visuals. We do not have a technical solution in place to perform this task automatically and across different partners accounts yet. 

Additionally, we’d likely need to review our image and content database to identify and delete any assets linked to partners who are no longer on the platform. Given the size and scope of our database, I’d prefer to avoid this if possible — but it’s important to clarify the expectations and legal obligations here.

Please let me know if there are any gaps in my understanding, and a painless way to resolve this issue and cost if we will stick to current approach.

About the issue. 

When superset been inited, from old doc I see it used such way to generate Secret key to work encrypt/decrypt data in postgres. 

{noformat}openssl rand -base64 42
EaYh7qTcP2YEoWtFw8R2Eks6EIhU6gp6iavjLbxMv5irxytpQgTKLnba{noformat}

The thing is, that decoding of this binary data.

{noformat}echo EaYh7qTcP2YEoWtFw8R2Eks6EIhU6gp6iavjLbxMv5irxytpQgTKLnba | base64 -d
�!��?f�kE��vK:�T�
z���-�L����+iB�.v�%{noformat}

So we have kinda this secret which later used by ENV in superset deployment. 

{noformat}        envFrom:
        - secretRef:
            name: apache-superset-extra-env
{noformat}

But in EKS 1.34, upgraded to newer version Golang which are using strict utf-8 check, as a result, container can’t start due to can’t validate string which passing as env to container. 

As fix, to not rotate secret key for superset, I create a new Sealed secret but as a base used not a Data in secret but stringData


{noformat}apiVersion: v1
stringData:
  SUPERSET_SECRET_KEY: �!��?f�kE��vK:�T�
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: apache-superset-extra-env
  namespace: apache-superset
type: Opaque{noformat}

With this, it’s able to start

[~accountid:712020:cd1584a2-01ac-4b9a-961f-699131bc6efd] I suppose the alternative you’re getting at is allowing a rider to pre-define what language(s) they want their driver to speak. A version of this is being testing in Croatia and Poland, but user sentiment around this is not great (it’s being dubbed “Bolt Xeno”). Discussion here: [https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C01NNFCCJJW/p1764756356731549|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C01NNFCCJJW/p1764756356731549|smart-link]

I think it’s safer to just match what our competitors are doing here — surfacing driver information without making any other changes. If a rider is matched with a driver and discovers they don’t speak their language, they can always cancel immediately with no penalty. 

But allowing riders to cherry-pick which drivers they want based on language can harm the rider experience (long ETAs) and lead to drivers feeling discriminated against. So it’s risky. At least, I haven’t seen any competitors do things this way.

Personally/anecdotally, I’d appreciate this information so that I know how to address drivers. If the driver only speaks English, I’ll say “Hello” — if the driver only speaks Estonia, then “Tere” — if only Russian, then “Privet”. Just saves the hassle of taking a guess and then awkwardly fumbling around until we understand each other’s language abilities. 

Relatedly, we should also show if the driver cannot communicate verbally:

[~accountid:712020:cd1584a2-01ac-4b9a-961f-699131bc6efd] we’ve heard reports that users are afraid to submit low ratings because they fear the driver may track them down and seek retribution (drivers know the rider’s name and address, usually). So in these cases, riders usually don’t leave a rating at all, and we never know there was any issue with the ride at all (CC [~accountid:712020:2f29b932-0bdf-4a3e-aa45-0ccbb584a767]).

Giving riders the ability to leave a high score but still manually unmatch is a kind of ‘back door’ for users to let us know the ride was actually not alright. And it’s a safety mechanism for riders in any case. 

But to be clear, our competitors do _not_ handle things this way. So I can’t be sure this is the right solution. 

I would like to test giving users control over manually unmatching, though, even if we restrict it only for 1- and 2-star ratings. I think it would be interesting to hear user feedback and see how/if they use it.

Rogers (via Red Wireless) has come back with a *redlined version of the Hopp Rewards partnership agreement*.

Overall, the proposed changes are *more tightly defined and structured* than our standard template. Given that Red Wireless has executed *multiple EPP (Exclusive Partnership Program) agreements in the Canadian market*, many of the changes appear *reasonable and in line with how they typically operate*, though there are some areas that tighten commitments on our side.

* *@Lisa / Legal* – could you please review the redlines from a legal standpoint and advise whether these changes are acceptable, or flag any areas of concern.
* *@Felix* – there are a few *commercial / business-side implications* (e.g. exclusivity, performance targets, term/termination) that we’ll need to discuss and align on separately.

*Timeline / urgency:*
This is a priority item. We’re targeting a *February launch for Hopp Rewards*, so we would ideally need contract review and signatures *by mid-January at the latest* to stay on track.

*Full redline document is here:* 👉 *[*[*LINK TO REDLINE DOC*|https://docs.google.com/document/d/17eK8dNrG4MdsqHhVYQVQ_tMaVxeo3KRd/edit?usp=sharing&ouid=103080997669308657183&rtpof=true&sd=true]*]*

Below are the bullet points of the changes:


*Red Wireless (Rogers) – Contract Redline Summary (for Legal)*

*Term & Termination*

* Initial *3-year term* with *auto 1-year renewals*; termination requires *90-day notice* before term end (removed ability to terminate freely on short notice).
* Cure period for material breach extended from *5 → 30 days*.
* New *performance-based termination right* for Partner if activation targets are missed *after remediation*.

*Exclusivity / Non-compete*

* Added *category exclusivity* during term *+ 6 months post-term* for:
** Wireless
** Home Internet
** Cable TV
(Only where Rogers/Red Wireless offers service in that jurisdiction.)
* Added *Rogers-specific non-circumvention*: Hopp cannot directly engage Rogers for a substantially similar program during term *+ 12 months post-term*.

*Governance & Commercial Commitments*

* Added requirement for a *joint Annual Strategic & Marketing Plan*.
* Added *mandatory Quarterly Business Reviews (QBRs)*.
* Appendix now mandates *minimum marketing touchpoints*, incl.:
** Launch email
** New-driver onboarding email
** Prominent in-app ranking (top 5 offers)
** Key retail moments (Black Friday, Boxing Week, etc.).

*Performance Targets (New)*

* Introduced *binding activation targets*:
** Year 1: *5,000 activations*
** Year 2+: *10,000 activations/year*
* Defined “activation” broadly (wireless, internet, TV, hardware upgrade each count).
* If targets missed → *formal remediation period* → Partner may terminate if unresolved.

*Changes to Control / Flexibility*

* *Removed Hopp’s unilateral right* to amend terms.
* All amendments now require *mutual written agreement*.

*IP & Branding*

* Tightened IP language:
** Hopp receives a *limited, revocable license* to use Partner/Rogers marks.
** Explicitly confirms *no perpetual rights*; all rights revert on termination.

*Data, Privacy & Confidentiality*

* Clarified that:
** Hopp may only use *de-identified / aggregated data* externally.
** *PII and Rogers customer data* remain strictly confidential.
* Added *QBR data-sharing obligations* (aggregated metrics only).
* Confidentiality obligations survive *3 years post-termination*.

*Dispute Resolution*

* Added *mandatory non-binding mediation in Toronto* before court proceedings.

*Liability & Indemnity*

* Liability carve-outs clarified for:
** Breach of confidentiality
** Fraud, bad faith, willful misconduct, negligence.
* Indemnities now explicitly *mutual*.

*Assignment*

* Assignment to affiliates or third parties now requires *prior written consent (not unreasonably withheld)*.

*Commercial Appendix (Offer Terms)*

* Wireless discount framed as *~$20 off consumer plans*.
* TV/Internet discounts left *TBD*.
* Redemption restricted to *online only*.
* Eligibility subject to *Rogers credit checks & service availability*.
* Territory explicitly Ontario + expansion by agreement.

Conducted some research and, in addition to the current test, found a few options to consider. We need to discuss some of these with the IoT team to determine their relevance.

Additional environment test:

Cyclic Corrosion Test (CCT)
CCT cycle (like *SAE J2334*) lasts 24 hours and repeats for 30–80 days

h4. *Stage 1: The Pollution Phase (Salt Mist)*

* *Action:* The chamber is filled with a fine salt fog.
* *Duration:* 15 minutes to 2 hours.
* *Conditions:* 35°C(95°F) with a 5% NaCl solution.
* *Goal:* To deposit a fresh layer of corrosive electrolyte over every surface, wire entry point, and cooling fin.

h4. *Stage 2: The High Humidity Phase (Soak)*

* *Action:* The spray stops, but the chamber stays at nearly 100% humidity.
* *Duration:* 6 to 8 hours.
* *Conditions:* 50°C (122°F) at 95-100% RH.
* *Goal:* To allow moisture to penetrate deep into the seals and "wick" the salt into the PCB via capillary action.

h4. *Stage 3: The Dry-Off Phase (The "Killer" Phase)*

* *Action:* Fresh, dry air is blown into the chamber to rapidly lower humidity.
* *Duration:* 4 to 8 hours.
* *Conditions:* 60°C (140°F) at <30% RH.
* *Goal:* This causes the salt to crystallize. As the crystals grow, they expand and can crack the conformal coating on the PCB or push past rubber gaskets.

h4. *Stage 4: The Ambient/Rest Phase*

* *Action:* The chamber returns to room temperature and humidity.
* *Duration:* Remaining hours of the day.
* *Goal:* Stabilizes the materials before the next thermal shock/spray cycle begins.

Life cycle tests:

* *Power Cycling Endurance:* Turning the system on and off 10,000+ times to test the inrush current management and the longevity of capacitors.
* *Continuous Load Test (Burn-in):* Running the controller at 80% capacity for 500+ hours in a high-temperature chamber (40°C).
* *Signal Endurance:* Repetitive "torture" of the throttle and brake signals (e.g., 50,000 pulses) to ensure the logic board doesn't glitch or freeze.

Sometimes, the payment is reversed without the bank sending a reversal notification to the customer, which might lead the user to think that the reversal has not been made.

The reversal can take up to *30 days* to complete, as pending authorisations typically expire after that time on banks end.

Unfortunately, we don't have full visibility into all the parties involved in the payment processing beyond our payment partner. Therefore, we can't track the exact status of the preauthorisation release once it has been sent.

Thank you,

Marten

As you may be aware, the right of access under data protection law does not provide an individual with an absolute right of full access to any and all information or documentation. Just one clarification from my side: when you mentioned that _“a threat received from a driver to the CS team need not result in suspension or termination unless it is a safety risk”_, what we are proposing here is that drivers who exhibit a *credible* suicidal threat (as defined in the draft document) should indeed be eligible for termination.



The argument is that credible suicidal behavior constitutes a safety risk, even if the driver does not explicitly direct that risk toward passengers or CS agents. A driver who demonstrates credible suicidal intent is, by definition, in an unstable and unpredictable mental state, and that unpredictability may pose danger to passengers or others while the driver is driving.



As a reminder, under the current guideline, any suicide threat (credible or not) is treated as a Significant safety event, with termination triggered after two occurrences. What this new guideline aims to do is allow termination after one credible suicide threat, for example in cases like the Thailand incident where the driver repeatedly contacted CS while sharing suicide notes and images of means (rope).



The intent is not to minimize or over-penalize suicide-related statements, but to ensure we act in clearly defined, high-severity safety situations where there is a legitimate safety concern. Happy to have a chat further if helpful!

Thank you for raising this.

In Portugal, requests from the Polícia de Segurança Pública (PSP) are considered valid when made within their legal powers, although they must still comply with the applicable legal framework. For this reason, the Legal team’s view is that PSP requests should be assessed on a case-by-case basis.
In this particular case, upon reviewing the attached notification, we note that a legal basis is indicated — specifically, in the box located at the bottom left corner of page two. The PSP references Article 6.º of the Código de Processo Penal (Criminal Procedural Code), which establishes that the PSP is competent to investigate crimes that are not within the exclusive competence of another criminal police authority, as well as any other cases assigned to them by the judicial authority.
The facts and crime under investigation (domestic violence) do not appear to fall within the reserved competence of another authority (e.g., Polícia Judiciária), meaning that the PSP does have the general competence to handle the matter and issue such a request.
That said, since the request involves the disclosure of personal data of a driver (name, ID doc, date of birth, personal address, contact, etc), we believe the Privacy team should also assess the request to ensure compliance with data protection rules.

Thank you!

Hey [~accountid:615c75e007ac3c0068114285] !
Thank you for raising this ticket.

We reviewed the policy and have a few items to align it with the original external and internal legal guidance and Privacy comments (you can find them [here|https://taxify.atlassian.net/browse/LSS-36226]).

Overall we think the policy is a good basis. However, we believe that the key point is that eligibility needs to be demonstrably based on _Maltese language proficiency_ (not nationality/birthplace), with clear storage/retention and a consistent verification process.

# *High-priority change* 

* The policy currently provides automatic registration for drivers “born in Malta” or holding “Maltese nationality” and assumes proficiency on that basis.
This is the main change we recommend removing, as it risks being perceived as a nationality proxy rather than a language-based eligibility criterion (which is exactly what external counsel flagged).
Proposal: make Rikba an opt-in category for all drivers, subject to the same verification route (declaration + certificate OR Ops assessment). If you want a “fast track”, base it on objective evidence (e.g., Maltese language qualification) rather than nationality/birthplace.

# *Make the language standard consistent*

* The policy mixes “basic/conversational/emergency” with an A2 requirement (currently applied only to “other drivers”).
Proposal: set one minimum standard for everyone (e.g., CEFR A2 spoken interaction or equivalent) and treat certificate / interview / video as acceptable ways to evidence it.

# *Privacy/retention clarifications*

To close out Privacy’s earlier questions, can you please add (even as an appendix):

* Exactly what data we collect/store (declaration text, certificate file, interview notes, beehive video, decision outcome).
* Where each item is stored (Admin field / ticket attachment / other) and who has access.
* Retention per item type (e.g., retain the declaration/certificate for duration of the driver account; if video is stored, propose a shorter retention period once verification is complete unless needed for disputes).

# *Complaint / re-assessment process*

* The annual/random checks section is a bit high-level. Please specify:
** triggers (e.g., substantiated complaint),
** what “random testing” means in practice,
** process and outcome (e.g., re-assessment → if fails, removal from Rikba only; no broader sanctions purely on language).

# *Quick implementation questions*

Since the policy doesn’t include the form/workflow text, can you please provide the concrete implementation details:

# Is auto-registration (born in Malta / nationality) currently implemented in product? If yes, can it be changed?
# Where exactly are certificates and beehive videos stored today? 
# Do you retain the full video, or only the verification outcome? If you keep video, what’s the retention period?
# What is the driver-facing declaration wording and any privacy notice shown at submission?
# What happens after a complaint? Is it only “remove Rikba tag,” or are there other consequences?

Yes, I’m aware of that and that’s the reason we need to use it like that. 

As starting from 01.01.2027 all companies must reference on the payments to the KSeF registration number (before that it’s obligatory, not mandatory). For the Suppliers that we are right now paying multiple invoices in one payment (mostly Market Grocery inventory Suppliers) there is a possibility in KSeF to request one Collective identifier KSeF number for all the invoices issued by that Supplier which you want to make one payment (even though maybe it would be easy to start making ‘always separate payments’ as this request is manual on based on the actual payment - so every time you are starting to make the payment you need to request this Collective identifier marking the exact invoices you are paying and then change the payment information in bank/Kyriba before approving the payment). That why it seems logical to use ‘Reference number’ field for KSeF registration number field. So that when the time comes (2027) we can turn on SEPA with Reference payments in PL in Kyriba.

Data prepared based on Carlos’s new query:

with
courier_balance as (
  select
iba.external_id as entity_id,
'courier' as entity_type,
sum(amount) as total_balance
from ng_payout_spark.invoicing_balance_balance_entry ibbe
left join ng_payout_spark.invoicing_balance_account iba on ibbe.account_id = [iba.id|http://iba.id]
left join ng_public_spark.admin_system_city sc on [sc.id|http://sc.id] = ibbe.city_id
where 1=1
and sc.country_code = 'bg'
and iba.type in ('food_courier', 'food_courier_cash')
group by 1
)
, courier_fleet_balance as (
select
iba.external_id as entity_id,
'courier_fleet' as entity_type,
sum(amount) as total_balance
from ng_payout_spark.invoicing_balance_balance_entry ibbe
left join ng_payout_spark.invoicing_balance_account iba on ibbe.account_id = [iba.id|http://iba.id]
left join ng_public_spark.admin_system_city sc on [sc.id|http://sc.id] = ibbe.city_id
where 1=1
and sc.country_code = 'bg'
and iba.type in ('delivery_fleet')
group by 1),
provider_balance as
(
select
iba.external_id as entity_id,
'provider' as entity_type,
sum(amount) as total_balance
from ng_payout_spark.invoicing_balance_balance_entry ibbe
left join ng_payout_spark.invoicing_balance_account iba on ibbe.account_id = [iba.id|http://iba.id]
left join ng_public_spark.admin_system_city sc on [sc.id|http://sc.id] = ibbe.city_id
where 1=1
and sc.country_code = 'bg'
and iba.type in ('food_restaurant', 'food_restaurant_credit')
group by 1
)
select * from courier_balance
union all
select * from courier_fleet_balance
union all
select * from provider_balance

This script in bolt-server folder helps to find matching:

{noformat}#!/bin/bash
# Helps to find mapping between redis name and CostCenter
set -euo pipefail

REDIS=$1 # redis name as single parameter
grep -B3 -A2 $REDIS config/redis/live.json

read -p "Bootstrap redis:? " BOOTSTRAP_REDIS
find src -type f -name "Bootstrap*.ts" -exec grep -H \"$BOOTSTRAP_REDIS\" {} \;

while True; do
        read -p "CODEOWNERS path:? " CODEOWNERS_PATH
        if ! grep $CODEOWNERS_PATH CODEOWNERS; then
                echo "Error: Path not found in CODEOWNERS, repeat"
        else
                break
        fi
done

while True; do
        read -p "CODEOWNER team:? (Ctrl+C to exit) " CODEOWNER
        jq "map_values(select(index(\"$CODEOWNER\")))" cost-center-codeowners.json
done{noformat}

The Rider app calls {{profile/auth/signout}} endpoint in the following cases ((/) is where the endpoint expected to be called and ❌ is where it’s not):

* (/) Explicit logout user action ([code|https://github.com/bolteu/android-app-client/blob/75dc234cc8922e0605ad90d2c7501a523ff5a061/modules/user/profile/src/main/java/eu/bolt/client/profile/rib/overview/ProfileOverviewRibInteractor.kt#L689-L705]).
* (/) Logout deeplink with a query param {{nosignoutcall=false}} ([code|https://github.com/bolteu/android-app-client/blob/ae16482164661f7d1ab9847ebd3d566fd30d2c31/app/src/main/java/ee/mtakso/client/ribs/root/loggedin/LoggedInDeeplinkHandler.kt#L127-L130]).
* ❌ Cancelling authentication flow ([code_1|https://github.com/bolteu/android-app-client/blob/34b5b78655e43691b8eb05755a7d6e8f26ac006d/modules/user/login/src/main/java/eu/bolt/client/login/rib/LoginFlowRibInteractor.kt#L566-L569], [code_2|https://github.com/bolteu/android-app-client/blob/34b5b78655e43691b8eb05755a7d6e8f26ac006d/modules/user/login/src/main/java/eu/bolt/client/login/rib/LoginFlowRibInteractor.kt#L561-L564], [code_3|https://github.com/bolteu/android-app-client/blob/59640a35f1bebe95f72585aec6b6ce8a423f2a1f/modules/user/login/src/main/java/eu/bolt/client/login/rib/postauth/PostAuthRibInteractor.kt#L115-L118]).
* ❌ {{mobility/appState/get/v1}} endpoint failed with one of the following codes ([code|https://github.com/bolteu/android-app-client/blob/34b5b78655e43691b8eb05755a7d6e8f26ac006d/modules/user/login/src/main/java/eu/bolt/client/login/rib/LoginFlowRibInteractor.kt#L457-L459]):
** {{NOT_AUTHORIZED}} - 503
** {{USER_NOT_FOUND}} - 10
** {{USER_CODE_NOT_CONFIRMED}} - 25
** {{USER_LOGIN_EXPIRED}} - 27
* ❌ When {{mobility/appState/get/v1}} endpoint failed with any other error code than the listed above, it causes to display an error dialog (eg. {{Please check your internet connection and try again}}). When the user closes the error dialog, the app calls the sign-out endpoint ([code_1|https://github.com/bolteu/android-app-client/blob/34b5b78655e43691b8eb05755a7d6e8f26ac006d/modules/user/login/src/main/java/eu/bolt/client/login/rib/LoginFlowRibInteractor.kt#L475] and [code_2|https://github.com/bolteu/android-app-client/blob/34b5b78655e43691b8eb05755a7d6e8f26ac006d/modules/user/login/src/main/java/eu/bolt/client/login/rib/LoginFlowRibInteractor.kt#L483]). This case explicitly excludes http network errors, only the error codes returned in this endpoint by our server.
* ❌ When locally cached user data is not found ([code|https://github.com/bolteu/android-app-client/blob/34b5b78655e43691b8eb05755a7d6e8f26ac006d/modules/user/login/src/main/java/eu/bolt/client/login/rib/LoginFlowRibInteractor.kt#L582-L584]).

As about the particular case of the user [277835853|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/identity/consumers/rider/277835853/overview] with the device_id {{dsWImmUbQ-WqU0jEVf1dlY}} it seems this is the case with the error dialog displayed after the appState endpoint call as in the [Mixpanel|https://mixpanel.com/project/1165336/view/32804/app/profile#distinct_id=$device:e1bff064-3d5b-4802-b31e-7de18af30b2d&~(dateRange~(type~'between~exclusionOffset~null~to~'2025-12-05T11*3a18*3a00~from~'2025-12-05T11*3a17*3a00))] I found that {{User Account Signout}} event preceded by  {{Error dialog}} event for the dialog with a message {{Please check your internet connection and try again}}. So here is the possible break down of what happened:

* The app was open by a deepklink (there is no data which one) as this is the first event before the issue happened.
* When the deeplink woke up the process, the process first called the appState endpoint
* The appState endpoint returned USER_LOGIN_EXPIRED which [triggered|https://github.com/bolteu/android-app-client/blob/a373752a936f688412e967c238503aeae50a7d01/core/src/main/java/ee/mtakso/client/core/interactors/user/FetchInitialAppStateSuspendingUseCase.kt#L105-L111] retry specifying that if the next attempt fails the retry is not needed.
* On the next attempt it returned USER_LOGIN_EXPIRED again and the attempt was not retried as requested. The error handling flow [fell down|https://github.com/bolteu/android-app-client/blob/a373752a936f688412e967c238503aeae50a7d01/core/src/main/java/ee/mtakso/client/core/interactors/user/FetchInitialAppStateSuspendingUseCase.kt#L119-L126] to the not authorized case (it treats all the error codes listed above as not authorized).
* This error handling flow sends an error event to the observers which doesn’t change anything for our issue, but it [re-throws|https://github.com/bolteu/android-app-client/blob/a373752a936f688412e967c238503aeae50a7d01/core/src/main/java/ee/mtakso/client/core/interactors/user/FetchInitialAppStateSuspendingUseCase.kt#L127] the error that makes to bubble it up to the upstream which was [here|https://github.com/bolteu/android-app-client/blob/34b5b78655e43691b8eb05755a7d6e8f26ac006d/modules/user/login/src/main/java/eu/bolt/client/login/rib/LoginFlowRibInteractor.kt#L314].
* The error handler in the upstream goes to [handleAuthStateFailed|https://github.com/bolteu/android-app-client/blob/34b5b78655e43691b8eb05755a7d6e8f26ac006d/modules/user/login/src/main/java/eu/bolt/client/login/rib/LoginFlowRibInteractor.kt#L451] which displays the error dialog and then eventually calls [logoutAndAttachSignInScreen|https://github.com/bolteu/android-app-client/blob/34b5b78655e43691b8eb05755a7d6e8f26ac006d/modules/user/login/src/main/java/eu/bolt/client/login/rib/LoginFlowRibInteractor.kt#L590] that under the hood calls the {{/profile/auth/signout}} endpoint.



If the RiderX team will implement the fix in scope of [https://taxify.atlassian.net/browse/RDXENG-4337|https://taxify.atlassian.net/browse/RDXENG-4337|smart-link], the scenario described above should be fixed too. The important is they fix all the places marked with ❌  in the list above as these use cases call the signout endpoint where it was not supposed to be called.

Advise the customer to *check with their bank* to confirm the release of the preauthorisation. Banks handle these releases differently, and while some are immediate, others may process it as a temporary charge that is then refunded. Sometimes, the payment is reversed without the bank sending a reversal notification to the customer, which might lead the user to think that the reversal has not been made.

The reversal can take up to *30 days* to complete, as pending authorisations typically expire after that time on banks end.

Unfortunately, we don't have full visibility into all the parties involved in the payment processing beyond our payment partner. Therefore, we can't track the exact status of the preauthorisation release once it has been sent.

Thank you,

Marten

Advise the customer to *check with their bank* to confirm the release of the preauthorisation. Banks handle these releases differently, and while some are immediate, others may process it as a temporary charge that is then refunded. Sometimes, the payment is reversed without the bank sending a reversal notification to the customer, which might lead the user to think that the reversal has not been made.

The reversal can take up to *30 days* to complete, as pending authorisations typically expire after that time on banks end.

Unfortunately, we don't have full visibility into all the parties involved in the payment processing beyond our payment partner. Therefore, we can't track the exact status of the preauthorisation release once it has been sent.

Thank you,

Marten

Following my review of the two payment errors involving Teleperformance (TP), I’ve summarised below the key facts, our legal position under the SOW, and the proposed next steps. Please could you review and let me know if you agree ? Thank you !



+*Case Overview*+

*Scenario 1 – €11,000 Payment to Incorrect Account*

* TP failed to verify that the bank account (RIB) belonged to the driver requesting a Bolt account. The driver is partially responsible for providing the wrong document.
* As a result, the €11,000 was directed to a third party in error.
* These were funds from passengers to drivers, with Bolt acting only as an intermediary. Thus, Bolt only suffered a limited direct financial loss because of the 11K EUR, we only reimbursed the driver of the amounts owed by Bolt approx. 200 EUR.
* The remaining amount is to be claimed by Bolt from the bank. 

*Scenario 2 – €13,000 Sent to Wrong Account and Repaid*

* TP again failed to correctly input/verify account details. This was entirely the fault of the TP agent.
* This led Bolt to send €13,000 to the wrong recipient. To ensure the rightful driver was paid, Bolt had to reissue another €13,000 from its own funds.
* We are now pursuing recovery from the mistaken beneficiary via an instalment plan.
* This error represents a direct financial loss to Bolt.



+*Legal Position*+

* *Breach of Contract*: TP was responsible under the SOW for verifying RIBs as part of its back-office services. Failure to do so is a breach of its obligations under Schedule 2.
* *Liability for Losses* (Schedule 6): TP is contractually required to fully compensate Bolt for any loss resulting from its breach. This applies to the €13K in Scenario 2.
* *Contractual Penalties*: Bolt may claim a penalty of up to €50,000 per breach if the claim is made within 60 days of discovering the breach.
* *Scenario 1* does not trigger a damages claim, but still represents a *performance failure* relevant for service credits, contractual escalation, or governance review.



+*Next Steps to be discussed with the business (their decision)*+

Inform the business of their options. Besides damages and penalties, the SOW may allow for:

# *Service credits* (especially for repeat quality issues)
# *Mandatory Service Improvement Plan (SIP)*
# *Escalation via governance meetings* (Schedule 11)
# *Right to terminate for material breach or negligence* (especially if this pattern continues)



If the business pushes for damages, next steps would be:

# *Confirm the discovery dates* of both incidents to assess penalty eligibility.
# *Issue a formal notice to TP*, demanding:
#* Full reimbursement of the €200 from Scenario 1 and €13,000 in Scenario 2;
#* Application of a contractual penalty (if within 60 days);
#* A corrective action plan to prevent further breaches.
# Consider escalation under the *governance or service improvement* provisions of the SOW.

→ Caveat to be highlighted: Bolt can claim damages from TP for the loss of revenue; however, if we successfully collect the mistaken funds from the third party (via instalment plan or via the bank), we will have to transfer the amounts back to TP, as we cannot have a double recovery. This method is still beneficial in order to compensate for our losses on the short term.

* Key general takeaways are as follows:
** No mandatory requirement to consult the IDPC when using the EU SCCs to transfer personal data out of Albania.
** “_Bolt should not request or retain criminal-record certificates from drivers. Instead, Bolt can lawfully verify suitability by (i) checking the validity and status of the driver’s taxi licenses and Taxi Driver Certificate, (ii) promptly deactivating drivers whose official authorisations are suspended or revoked_”. This is because drivers already undergo criminal record vetting when obtaining their Taxi Driver Certificate and taxi service licences.
*** I should check with Local Ops whether we intend to collect criminal record certifications ⚠️ If not, then this is fine.
** If Bolt is conducting profiling (including compiling ‘interest profiles’: “_a profile of an identifiable individual’s likely preferences or usage patterns, created through automated or semi-automated analysis of personal data (e.g., ride history, app interactions, stated preferences) to personalise features, recommendations, or communications_”), transparency duty applies. However, Bolt only needs to disclose “_meaningful information about the logic involved_” and the “_significance and envisaged consequences_” for the data subject if it is ADM producing legal/significant effects.
* Key marketing takeaways are as follows:
** Opt-in consent is not required in the following scenarios:
*** Bolt is sending Bolt marketing to Bolt users (via channels other than email/SMS) and no SCD is involved (i.e., soft opt-in).
*** Bolt is sending third-party marketing to Bolt users (via channels other than email/SMS) and: (i) data being processed is not SCD/criminal data; (ii) data was collected directly by Bolt, together with clear notice that it may be used to send third-party marketing (or it was sourced from publicly accessible sources); and (iii) the user has an unconditional right to object at all times.
*** Bolt is sending Bolt marketing to third party’s customers (via channels other than email/SMS) and: (i) data must be limited to name, gender, age group and address; (ii) third party must have informed the customers at the time of collection that their data must be used for other controllers' direct marketing; and (iii) customer must have an unconditional right to object at all times.
** Opt-in consent is required in the following scenarios:
*** Bolt is sending Bolt (or third-party) marketing to Bolt users (or third party’s customers) via email or SMS.
**** Although soft opt-in exception applies in Albania, A9 of the e-Commerce Law does not permit the sending of promotional comms by email/SMS without consent. This law does not have extraterritorial effect (and so would not apply to Bolt if the sending entity is not based in Albania); however, the conservative approach recommended by external advisors is to treat A9 as the practical standard for email/SMS to Albanian users (although this interplay has not yet been tested in practice). External advisors recommended consulting with the IDPC to get its view on this issues.
**** This would require a chance to DM practices. Worth considering consulting with the IDPC ⚠️ 
*** Bolt is sending third-party marketing to Bolt users and the above requirements are not met.
*** Bolt is sending Bolt marketing to third party’s customers and the above requirements are not met.
** Comms sent to generic corporate email addresses should not trigger the above requirements (i.e., B2C, not B2B). However, this has not yet been formally tested by regulators, so treat with caution.

I think it is easier to explain through the same examples that I included in the previous response. 

For example one: invoice C-DE001-23-000024 - the invoice was for amount EUR 1,500. Later, the invoice was adjusted with a credit note also for the same amount EUR 1,500. In other words, the invoice was not paid, but was closed with a credit note. The status of the invoice in Column K should not say “Paid” as this is misleading. Could the status say “Credit Note” ? Equally Column M and N state that the invoice was settled, which is also misleading. Column M and N should only contain data if a cash payment is received. 

For example three: invoice C-DE001-23-000045 - the invoice was for amount EUR 304.17. Later, the invoice was written off for the same amount EUR 304.17. In other words, the invoice was not paid, but was closed with a write off. The status of the invoice in Column K should not say “Paid” as this is misleading. Could the status say “Written off” ? Equally Column M and N state that the invoice was settled, which is also misleading. Column M and N should only contain data if a cash payment is received. 

The report should continue to show the adjustments and write-offs, but column K should state “Paid” only when a cash settlement occurs and columns for Settlement (currently M-P) should only contain data if a cash settlement occurs. 

I hope this clarifies the request. Happy to provide more information if required.

I've reviewed the case and everything is correct on Bolt's end. The preauthorisation was successfully released, and there is no further action required from us.

Advise the customer to *check with their bank* to confirm the release of the preauthorisation. Banks handle these releases differently, and while some are immediate, others may process it as a temporary charge that is then refunded. Sometimes, the payment is reversed without the bank sending a reversal notification to the customer, which might lead the user to think that the reversal has not been made.

The reversal can take up to *30 days* to complete, as pending authorisations typically expire after that time on banks end.

Unfortunately, we don't have full visibility into all the parties involved in the payment processing beyond our payment partner. Therefore, we can't track the exact status of the preauthorisation release once it has been sent.
