Hi [~accountid:712020:b3dbddb5-16a8-4ad6-9138-80fbe6e695a9], I think that we should proactively offer some options to the business to allow them to make an informed decision regarding St Ouen.

+For context+: Bolt signed a commercial lease effective 01.01.2024 but has not occupied the premises due to a regulatory requirement mandating structural assessments and potential structural compliance works to open the site to the public (ERP classification). This requirement, stemming from building regulations, was not unforeseeable and thus does not qualify for a _force majeure_ or _imprévision defense_.

# *Premises Acceptance and Use Limitations (Article 1)* Bolt contractually acknowledged having visited and accepted the premises as suitable for its needs. This precludes a claim based on unfitness for purpose unless the landlord actively misrepresented the property’s compliance status. Given the public ERP use was foreseeable, responsibility for assessing such compliance likely falls on Bolt or any advisor it engaged.
# *Lease Duration and Termination Rights (Article 2)* The lease follows the standard 3/6/9 format under Article L145-4 of the French Commercial Code. It began on 01.01.2024, and the earliest contractual termination date is 31.12.2026. To exercise this right, Bolt must notify the landlord by registered letter with acknowledgment of receipt (_LRAR_) or by _huissier_ *no later than 30.06.2026*. Early termination before this date is only possible through a negotiated agreement or transfer to a third party.
# *Insurance Coverage (Article 14)* Bolt is obligated to maintain insurance under the lease. The insurance policy should be obtained and reviewed to determine whether coverage exists for business interruption or non-occupancy due to regulatory non-compliance. If coverage exists, a claim should be initiated to recover any ongoing losses.
# *Sublease or Assignment Options (Article 15)* Subleasing is permitted only in full and subject to prior written consent of the landlord. Assignment is also possible, but Bolt remains jointly liable for three years following the transfer under Article L145-16 of the Commercial Code. Bolt should begin market testing to identify potential tenants or assignees who may have different use requirements not subject to ERP constraints, and initiate landlord discussions.
# *Exit by Negotiation* Bolt may propose an early release from the lease through a negotiated agreement. The landlord may require an indemnity for early departure. A commercial proposal can be submitted outlining Bolt’s inability to use the space and the lack of market utility to support a fair settlement.
# *Broker Liability Consideration* If Bolt relied on a broker or advisor who failed to flag ERP compliance obligations or assess the regulatory status of the premises, a claim for professional negligence may be considered. This would require documentation of the broker's mandate, role, and any written advice or omissions. Without such documents currently in hand, this avenue remains speculative but should not be ruled out.
# *Immediate Action Items*

* Serve termination notice by 30.06.2026 to end lease on 31.12.2026.
* Review insurance policy and consult broker to assess potential claims.
* Identify prospective subtenants or assignees for full transfer.
* Engage landlord for potential negotiated early termination.
* Compile any documentation evidencing reliance on third-party advice.

*Conclusion* Bolt is bound to the lease until 31.12.2026 unless it negotiates an early exit or transfers the lease. The structural compliance requirement does not justify unilateral termination. +*UPDATE*+

* Updated marketing takeaways from the Q&A with external advisors ([LINK|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1zq_BbpVgRUDBhI0oz4mgaXNMrRwRoiHd/edit]):
** Opt-in consent is not required in the following scenarios:
*** Bolt is sending Bolt marketing to Bolt users (via channels other than email/SMS) and no SCD is involved (i.e., soft opt-in).
*** Bolt is sending third-party marketing to Bolt users (via channels other than email/SMS) and: (i) data being processed is not SCD/criminal data; (ii) data was collected directly by Bolt, together with clear notice that it may be used to send third-party marketing (or it was sourced from publicly accessible sources); and (iii) the user has an unconditional right to object at all times.
*** Bolt is sending Bolt marketing to third party’s customers (via channels other than email/SMS) and: (i) data must be limited to name, gender, age group and address; (ii) third party must have informed the customers at the time of collection that their data must be used for other controllers' direct marketing; and (iii) customer must have an unconditional right to object at all times.
** Opt-in consent is required in the following scenarios:
*** Bolt is sending Bolt (or third-party) marketing to Bolt users (or third party’s customers) via email or SMS.
**** Although soft opt-in exception applies in Albania, A9 of the e-Commerce Law does not permit the sending of promotional comms by email/SMS without consent. This law does not have extraterritorial effect (and so would not apply to Bolt if the sending entity is not based in Albania); however, the conservative approach recommended by external advisors is to treat A9 as the practical standard for email/SMS to Albanian users (although this interplay has not yet been tested in practice). External advisors recommended consulting with the IDPC to get its view on this issues.
*** Bolt is sending Bolt (or third-party) marketing to Bolt users (or third party’s customers) and SCD/criminal data is involved.
*** Bolt is sending third-party marketing to Bolt users and the above requirements are not met.
*** Bolt is sending Bolt marketing to third party’s customers and the above requirements are not met.
** Comms sent to generic corporate email addresses should not trigger the above requirements. This is because Instruction No.4 states that DM applies to comms with “_directly identifiable persons_”. As such, B2B marketing is not caught. However, this has not yet been formally tested by regulators, so treat with caution.
* Based on my own research:
** Instruction No.4 of 30 April 2025 ([LINK|https://idp.al/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/Guideline-No.04-30.04.2025-Direct-Marketing.pdf]):
*** Aligns with the above.
** E-Commerce Law 2009 ([LINK|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1frbgBZ6vmC01hUFmUWK63PKyOzowsKxo/edit]):
*** Application of the Law:
**** Article 5: Applies to information society service providers either established in, or with a registered office in, Albania. 
**** This law does not have extraterritorial effect. In the case of the localised model (which applies here), they would likely apply to the Bolt Partner. There is no official guidance or settled administrative/judicial practice on applying these provisions to cross-border platforms targeting Albanian users, and to date Albanian authorities appear to have refrained from enforcing them extraterritorially. 
**** However, this law is aligned with the e-Commerce Directive (whereby core consumer-information duties are, in principle, expected to be met). External advisors recommended that Bolt should comply as a matter of prudence / maintaining user trust.
*** If the business' position is that we should strictly comply (TBC), the main requirements are as follows (see Chapter III):
**** Article 8: Must be clearly identifiable as promotional comms, must clearly state the identity of the sender.
**** Article 9: Unsolicited promotional comms by email or SMS are permitted only with the recipient’s prior consent, and the provider must keep a register of opt-outs.
* Thoughts:
** Current Bolt standard for sending DM marketing (i.e., rely on soft opt-in for Bolt marketing, and ‘partner offers’ consent for third-party marketing) should be fine in Albania, except for sending Bolt marketing via email/SMS (the _conservative_ approach is to obtain consent here, rather than the soft opt-in). 
*** However, the threat of sanctions here seems hypothetical, and the recommendation to rely on opt-in consent for email/SMS is more a matter of good practice than being objectively mandatory. Also, local law (Instruction No.4 of 30 April 2025) says that Bolt can rely on the soft opt-in for sending its own direct marketing. This law does not contain any carve-out for emails/SMS. This suggests we may be able to continue with the standard approach on a risk basis.
** Next steps:
*** Check with the business: (i) which entity will be sending DM here (it will either be Bolt Ops OU, or local partner - in either case, Bolt would not be explicitly caught, but the nexus would be even more tenuous if the local partner (as controller) is sending the comms); and (ii) what specific language we will be using to collect marketing consents (this is more of a ‘for good measure’ point).
*** Check with Regional Legal for their conclusions re e-Commerce law compliance ([link|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/D09BUPJRFQ8/p1767364502125729]). If other stakeholder teams are adopting a risk-based approach, it would make sense for us to do the same.
*** Double-check the application of Law 54/2024 on Electronic Communications.
*** Depending on the outcome, consider if opt-in consent will be needed for Bolt emails (as in Poland).
*** Update DM guidance on confluence.

+*UPDATE (05.12)*+

* Legal position:
** Under Albanian law, data on criminal convictions and offences are a distinct, specially protected category (though not SCD). In practice, Bolt can only process it if it is expressly authorised by Albania law - consent alone is not enough to legitimise it.
** In the specific context of driver registrations (which is the main context):
*** Per external advisor advice: “_Bolt should not request or retain criminal-record certificates from drivers. Instead, Bolt can lawfully verify suitability by (i) checking the validity and status of the driver’s taxi licenses and Taxi Driver Certificate, (ii) promptly deactivating drivers whose official authorisations are suspended or revoked_”. 
*** This is because drivers already undergo criminal record vetting when obtaining their Taxi Driver Certificate and taxi service licences.
* Expected Bolt practices:
** Per “_current Albanian practice_” ([link|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1OKGcIud5ukWUntpsZrpp9mae6ozkVoO-/edit]), Platform Operators apparently should collect a “_criminal record certificate_” and a “_medical certificate_” as part of onboarding. No _statutory_ requirement for Bolt to do this. Some municipalities also require periodic re-submission.
*** NB. Under the Localised model, the Partner would be the platform operator.
** I have asked the business if we have a good reason for collecting these documents [here|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C09258PDYE9/p1767605626101269].
*** Business mentioned n passing that this issue (among others) would be addressed when we reach the driver funnel stage.
* Thoughts / Next Steps:
** It sounds like we are unlikely to have a legal basis for collecting criminal records data (unless we have a clear and legal reason for doing so). As such, when we reach the driver funnel stage, the steps will be as follows (i) 
*** 1. Flag to the business that we can only collect criminal records data if we are expressly authorised to do so by law. ‘Standard practice’ has very little bearing on this.
*** 2. Ask the business if we are collecting these documents due to a specific legal obligation. Flag that drivers already undergo a criminal record check when obtaining their Taxi Driver Certificate.
*** 3. Advise that we should not be collecting these docs if there is not a compelling basis for doing so.
*** 4. If we go ahead with collecting them anyway, consider a DPIA and retention/anonymisation advice.
** NB. Re the collection of medical certificates, requirements here align with the GDPR.
*** 1. Flag to the business that we should only collect this if strictly necessary. Push the business on why exactly we need this.
*** 2. If this is strictly necessary, then most likely basis would be consent (or if explicitly authorised by law - see [here|https://www.karanovicpartners.com/news/albania-adopts-new-instruction-on-the-processing-of-health-and-genetic-data/#:~:text=2)%2C%20on%20the%20protection%20of,unless%20explicitly%20provided%20by%20law.]). If we get to this point, it is worth considering how we do this in other countries. We would also need to consider retention / anonymisation where no longer strictly necessary. Also, DPIA.
** Also NB.: The business has not yet been fully informed of the risks here, as it is unclear whether we are going ahead with it. I previously asked [here|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C09258PDYE9/p1767605626101269], but was told this would be considered at the driver funnel stage (see [comment|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1cSVqm64eozm1R7uaHHUNjf7IDfcq1x3BO1yKhT-YydM/edit?tab=t.0] from Jan 6: “_Once agreement is signed, we'd move into agreeing on the driver funnel, including sign-offs from Privacy, Legal, etc._”).

I have notes from the previous year of different thoughts:

* Public attack surface should be grouped roughly by technical domain / foundation-platform area
* In AWS, a few queries can be used:
** AWS EC2 instances living in bolt-vpc “public” subnets with assigned public ipv4 address and a security group allowing access from non-private IPv4 addresses
*** Without these last 2 filters you get a lot of False Positives
** AWS RDS instances with public endpoints and a permissive security group
** AWS Application & Network Load Balancers
** AWS API Gateway APIs
** AWS CloudFront Distributions
** AWS S3 buckets with no _Block Public Access_ or _Network Path Policies_ set up
** Public AWS DynamoDB Tables 
** Public AWS AMIs
* However, roughly we can look at how our cloud owners work and work backwards from there.
** SRE Cloud: 
*** Our OpenVPN infrastructure is in {{networking}} (3 openvpn VMs with port 1194 open to the world)
** SREP & Web & WAVE:
*** Web & other teams use CloudFront & S3 heavily, with older S3 setups not using CloudFront Origin Access Controls
*** Our EKS API servers are normally private, except for one that used to be needed for Presto
*** Application servers are often behind AWS ALB & ACM for automatic TLS termination, so load balancers need to be reviewed as wel
** DBRE:
*** Usually in a bolt-vpc strict subnet, but can use the proxy to access the Internet and regional data servers
* Some Steampipe queries that can be interesting to see:



Find EC2 instances with suspicious security group rules:

{code:sql}-- Find EC2 instances based on their security group rules
-- NOTE: before use, modify the WHERE clauses (e.g. removing the account ID filter)
with 
	security_group_expanded as (
		select 
			group_id, 
			jsonb_array_elements(ip_permissions) ->> 'FromPort' as from_port, 
			jsonb_array_elements(ip_permissions) ->> 'ToPort' as to_port, 
			(jsonb_array_elements(jsonb_array_elements(ip_permissions) -> 'IpRanges') ->> 'CidrIp') :: cidr as cidr_ip 
		from 
			aws_all.aws_vpc_security_group
	),
	instances as (
		select 
			sp_ctx, 
			account_id, 
			instance_id, 
			public_ip_address, 
			tags ->>'Name' as name,

+*Update 05.01.2026*+

* I reviewed why the pre-analysis was not holding for in-house experiments and found that the false positive rate over the past six months has been unstable.
* Further investigation showed this was largely due to a low probability impact threshold (80%), which resulted in many random impacts being detected without any intervention. Increasing the threshold to 90% partially resolved the issue, but the false positive rate remained close to the limit.
* To address this further, I increased the training period to 56 days (from 28), raised {{prior_level_SD}} to 0.15 across all markets, and introduced weekly seasonality into the CI. These changes significantly improved results across most markets and reduced flat predictions to nearly zero.

*Next Steps*

* I will monitor {{prior_level_SD}} values of 0.1 and 0.05 to see if sensitivity can be improved further while keeping the false positive rate low.

[~accountid:712020:cd1584a2-01ac-4b9a-961f-699131bc6efd] So this is on the ride category screen, before booking (switching payment after booking isn’t possible except in some unique cases like APM–>Cash and insufficient balance, I think). Based on feedback, what happens is:

* Users go to book a ride — see available categories and prices
* Before booking, users realise the payment method is wrong and update it
* After updating payment method, they see available categories and prices again — but now the prices have changed
* Users get confused and wonder why

So the idea was to give some explanation about why the price changed so they don’t feel like we’re a scammy company that’s just trying to trick them into spending more (btw prices can also go down, but of course users don’t really notice/mind/care about this).

One option we discussed was just to lock prices and avoid these kinds of price changes entirely. But as I recall, this was too complex as it also affects incentives and discounts — very messy and costly for us. 

I think a hybrid approach is best: make sure prices never change for new users only ([https://taxify.atlassian.net/jira/polaris/projects/RDS/ideas/view/7257850?selectedIssue=RDS-1190&issueViewSection=comments|https://taxify.atlassian.net/jira/polaris/projects/RDS/ideas/view/7257850?selectedIssue=RDS-1190&issueViewSection=comments|smart-link]) and provide a short explanation for everyone else. [~accountid:712020:cd1584a2-01ac-4b9a-961f-699131bc6efd] I’ve edited the description to remove the focus on elderly and visually impaired riders. I think it’s a distraction. This should be an improvement for all users and is basic feature parity with comp. 

And it overlaps nicely with expanded accessibility features for drivers who may be deaf or hard of hearing. Right now, riders can’t see this info, so many try calling the driver, but the driver obviously can’t talk on the phone. So it creates delays, frustration, and awkwardness. 

Knowing how to communicate with a driver (both the preferred language and preferred medium) will lead to smoother rides for many users.

The time to accept an order is fixed at 15 seconds for most markets. Matching team did an AB test last year and moved it from 20 seconds to 15 seconds.

[~accountid:712020:cd1584a2-01ac-4b9a-961f-699131bc6efd] So as I understand:

* Standard order — Rider makes a request, it is sent to 1 nearby driver (algorithmically determined), and driver has -~20- 15 seconds to accept or decline. If they decline, the order goes to the next driver, and the process repeats until the order is accepted or times out.
* Blast dispatch — This involves sending 1 order to numerous drivers at once. The first driver to accept gets the order, the rest do not. There is no 15-second wait and, in fact, these orders are usually accepted extremely quickly (common driver feedback is that they didn’t even have a chance to read the order details before another driver grabs it). 
* Driver tinder — This is mainly a rider feature. It involves showing riders nearby drivers and allowing riders to pick their preferred driver (rather than algorithmic allocation). I believe this is only live in Portugal and only for legal reasons. Overall, it does not create the best user experience. Not related to this ticket. 
* Price bidding — This involves showing a driver a list of offers from riders, and allowing the driver to accept or counter various offers at the same time. But this concept is wholly different from the rapid-fire requests in the original video, which is the problem I’m trying to solve here. 

So overall, it’s standard orders + (maybe) blast dispatch that’s causing the problem. A 3-second cooldown would allow drivers to handle basic app functions (like going offline, setting a destination, taking a break) without constant interruption from new orders.

+*BACKGROUND*+

* In Albania, we are required to implement real-time API integration of certified invoicing software with the *tax authority’s* server (invoice data is sent electronically per transaction).
** i.e., Per Law No. 87/2019, if the Platform handles payments directly, for tax purposes its billing software must integrate via API with the tax authority’s system.
** See section 6 of this memo ([link|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1JKYzalU52Iya3-rmfE9EUEe_le6NZ1J3/edit]), as well as tax memo feedback ([link|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1pYw2lSBCg3kuHnKgYP6G0nic2OFd7TzO/edit]).
* NB. No similar obligation for API integration with other transport authorities. Yet some municipalities ask for driver & vehicle rosters electronically at renewal, and Bolt must generally comply with authorities.

+*THOUGHTS*+

* *Legal Basis / Proportionality*: If this is legally mandatory, then we should be covered on both counts ✅ 
* *Transparency*: PNs mention that we share certain information with tax authorities, so we can argue this is covered ✅ 
* *Agreements*: Ideally, we would have a DSA in place. It seems very unlikely that we would be able to negotiate our own template, since the API integration sounds like standard practice in Albania. However, worth checking what data sharing provisions (if any) are already in place (?) 
** I have asked with the latest status on this (including re agreements) is [here|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C09258PDYE9/p1767605626101269].

Hi [~accountid:712020:75cc9b72-db8b-4dff-9671-3ed8fde897df]  

*I reissued the invoice several times → But invoice still comes out with incorrect data?*

If you reissue an invoice several times and it gets fiscalised with a VAT code at least once (ie you get an invoice with a QR) → whatever newly reissued (with a different VAT code) invoices will not get fiscalised.

Therefore invoices get stuck with incorrect (old fiscalised) data.

*What is the solution?*

We investigate with the provider if there is a workaround for it. However, it is not a high priority change as of now.

*What to do now?*

From now on please make sure that you reissue invoices to the correct Data (correct VAT code).

Best regards,

Nikolay Roll

The respond from BNB:

_Thank you for the clarification and the specific examples. I have reviewed these cases with the technical team to see how we can align the report with your requirements._
_However, I must clarify some system limitations regarding how Workday processes these transactions:_
_Status (Column K): In Workday, the "Paid" status is a system-default trigger. When an adjustment or a write-off is applied to fully offset an invoice, the system automatically transitions the status to "Paid" to indicate the balance is now zero. Unfortunately, we cannot customize this specific status field to say "Credit Note" or "Written off" as it is hardcoded in the core logic of the platform._

_Settlement Columns (M & N): Similarly, when the invoice balance reaches zero via an adjustment, Workday records that date and amount as the "Settlement" event. The system considers the invoice "settled" (closed) even if no cash was exchanged._
_The Solution: To distinguish between actual cash payments and accounting adjustments, we have included specific columns in the report for Adjustments and Write-offs._
_My recommendation for your analysis is to filter these columns:_
_Any row where the "Adjustment" or "Write-off" column has a value indicates that the "Paid" status was reached via an accounting move, not cash._
_If those columns are empty and the status is "Paid," you can be certain it was a cash settlement._
_I understand this might require an extra step in your review process, but it is the most reliable way to report this data given Workday’s standard architecture._
_Please let me know if you would like me to help you set up these filters or if you need further clarification on these columns._

Hello [~accountid:712020:d008dcec-6cfe-47e4-83a0-c29522744742] , find below the answers to the various questions you brought up. Do not hesitate to reach out, if you need further clarifications.

*1.Nature and duration of blockings*
All blockings are *temporary* in nature. An initial blocking is imposed for a period of *three (3) days*. Should a driver, following the completion of this initial blocking, accumulate *more than five (5) warnings*, a subsequent blocking of *seven (7) days* will be applied.

*2. Rating calculation methodology*
On a weekly basis, a call list is generated identifying drivers whose ratings fall within the *4.0 to 4.5 range*. Driver ratings are calculated based on *ratings submitted by riders in connection with completed trips*.

*3. Verification and investigation of low ratings*
 Low ratings are *not subject to formal verification or investigation* prior to the issuance of a warning or the application of a blocking. When a driver is identified on the call list, an agent contacts the driver to issue a warning based on one or more of the following factors:

* Written comments provided by riders on the driver’s profile
* Problem-category indicators selected by riders
* Instances of low driver activity

*4.Consideration of negative rider comments associated with low ratings*

Negative comments submitted by riders, including those associated with low ratings, are utilised for *informational and corrective purposes only*. Such comments are referenced by agents during driver communications to *educate, sensitise, and encourage improvement in driver conduct and performance*.

*5. Driver population potentially impacted by the proposed five-warning policy*
 Approximately *1,300 drivers* currently fall within the *4.0–4.5 rating range weekly*. Of this group, an estimated *500 drivers* may be impacted by the implementation of the suspension.

The proposed new blocking initiative was submitted to Julien Mouyeket, who expressed a favorable view. Final implementation remains subject to your review and approval.

Hey, [~accountid:60f2a71843c956007065f2ad]! Thank you for reaching out. I have started my review with answering your question regarding article 2 of the new act regarding the vehicles that are exempt from registration because this determines whether or not the act will be relevant to Bolt.

The Article 2 of the act provides several exemptions from which I find 2 that can be potentially relevant for Bolt (I removed irrelevant wording):

* Article 2 (1): two-wheeled vehicles with an electric motor having a maximum designed speed above 25 km/h that don’t have a seat, or which have a seat that does not allow R-point to exceed 540 mm, which have a weight not exceeding 50 kg. 
* Article 2 (2): two-wheeled vehicles with an electric motor having a maximum designed speed above 6 km/h, but not exceeding 25 km/h that don’t have a seat, or which have a seat that does not allow R-point to exceed 540 mm, which have a weight equal to or exceeding 50 kg. 

Since e-scooter does not have a seat we can also disregard the part about R-point, which leaves us with this criteria that we need to satisfy to benefit from the exemption:

* maximum designed speed above 25 km/h, but weight not exceeding 50 kg.
* maximum designed speed up to 25 km/h, but weight exceeding 50 kg.

As far as I am aware our e-scooters weight below 50kg, but the maximum designed speed is above 25 km/h, which is not a problem since we fit the exemption under Article 2 point 1.

Using DeepL (see attached), I have now reviewed the insurance contract with Transmagistral from an insurance perspective. 

Overall, the structure and scope appear appropriate for the Private Driver / Driver-only category in Ukraine as outlined in this ticket [+LSS-52953+ |https://taxify.atlassian.net/browse/LSS-52953]and are consistent with the legal analysis already obtained for this service.

The policy seems to address the issue of insuring the user’s own vehicle damages during a driver-only trip, which is not covered by mandatory Motor Third Party Liability (MTPL). 

Any third-party property damage and bodily injury should be covered under the vehicle’s MTPL, which follows the vehicle rather than the driver under Ukrainian law. So there is no risk of duplication of cover and no unintended shift of liability to us.

The limits, per-ride pricing (UAH 50 per completed trip), territorial scope, and aggregate structure all seem consistent with the intended use case and local market practices. Therefore, from an insurance structuring perspective, I do not see any issues that would prevent us from proceeding.

However, it is worth highlighting that the coverage is narrow and that claims handling will be procedural and insurer-driven (including police reporting requirements, strict notification timelines, and potentially extended decision periods). While this is standard locally, it will require clear internal and user-facing expectation management. The coverage is also dependent on timely and accurate monthly reporting and premium settlement, which the business will need to ensure is managed appropriately. 

It is also worth flagging the scenario where a vehicle owner does not have any MTPL. In such cases, third-party damage would be uninsured at vehicle level, with liability sitting with the vehicle owner and/or driver personally. Ukraine does have a compensation fund via MTIBU for damage caused by uninsured vehicles, but this is limited, procedural, and subject to recovery action against the responsible parties. The Transmagistral policy does not respond to third-party damage and would not mitigate this scenario. I am not the legal person in the room, but if we allow an uninsured vehicle to be driven via our platform and it hits someone or something; I am not sure if under Ukrainian law if we can be help vicariously liable for this? 

Therefore, from a risk management perspective, the business needs to ensure we have frameworks and procedures to ensure compliance with mandatory MTPL. (e.g. whether this is based solely on user representations in the T&Cs, or whether any form of verification is envisaged), and which team owns this check operationally.

Lastly, I have only just looked at this so all the process and verifications may have already been discussed; however, if you need me or my team to be involved in the reporting, claims, invoicing etc it will need to be discussed. 

Separately, and for future reference, this placement appears to have been arranged directly with the local insurer. 

I do not want to be seen as delaying this and asking for it to be revisited. However, for similar things going forward it would be good to involve our local broker earlier for market benchmarking and governance consistency and has Transmagistral gone through supplier assessments and procurement processes. 

Lastly, it would also be helpful to clarify the budget ownership for the ongoing per-trip insurance cost, as this is not currently shown in the tickets and has not been factored into my budgets.

Advise the customer to *check with their bank* to confirm the release of the preauthorisation. Banks handle these releases differently, and while some are immediate, others may process it as a temporary charge that is then refunded. Sometimes, the payment is reversed without the bank sending a reversal notification to the customer, which might lead the user to think that the reversal has not been made.

The reversal can take up to *30 days* to complete, as pending authorisations typically expire after that time on banks end.

Unfortunately, we don't have full visibility into all the parties involved in the payment processing beyond our payment partner. Therefore, we can't track the exact status of the preauthorisation release once it has been sent.

+*UPDATE (05.01.26)*+

* Feedback received on DM Q&A last year (there was a miscommunication with stakeholders) in this document ([+LINK+|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1zq_BbpVgRUDBhI0oz4mgaXNMrRwRoiHd/edit]). Key DM updates are as follows:
** Opt-in consent is +*not*+ required for the following direct marketing comms:
*** (a) Bolt is sending *Bolt* marketing to *Bolt* users (via channels other than email/SMS) and no SCD is involved (i.e., we can rely on soft opt-in).
*** (b) Bolt is sending *third-party* marketing to *Bolt* users (via channels other than email/SMS) and: (i) data being processed is not SCD/criminal data; (ii) data was collected directly by Bolt, together with clear notice that it may be used to send third-party marketing (or it was sourced from publicly accessible sources); and (iii) the user has an unconditional right to object at all times.
*** (c) Bolt is sending *Bolt* marketing to *third party’s* customers (via channels other than email/SMS) and: (i) data must be limited to name, gender, age group and address; (ii) third party must have informed the customers at the time of collection that their data must be used for other controllers' direct marketing; and (iii) customer must have an unconditional right to object at all times.
**** NB. This is broader than the soft opt-in exception, as it allows us to dispense with consent for third-party marketing where proper notice is provided.
** There is a +*grey area*+ regarding whether opt-in consent is required for the following direct marketing comms:
*** (a) Bolt (as a non-Albania entity) is sending Bolt (or third-party) marketing to Bolt users (or to third party’s customers) *via email or SMS*.
**** Although soft opt-in exception applies in Albania, A9 of the e-Commerce Law does not permit the sending of promotional comms by email/SMS without consent (this is a channel-specific requirement).
**** +However+, this law does not have extraterritorial effect (and so would not apply to Bolt if the sending entity is not based in Albania). Also, the interplay between A9 and local requirements has not ben tested in practice.
**** +Nevertheless+, the *_conservative_* approach (recommended by external advisors). is to treat A9 as the practical standard for email/SMS to Albanian users. The external advisors recommended consulting with the IDPC to get its view on this issue.
** Opt-in consent +*is*+ otherwise required for the following direct marketing comms:
*** (a) Bolt is sending Bolt (or third-party) marketing to Bolt users (or third party’s customers) and *SCD/criminal data* is involved.
*** (b) Bolt is sending third-party marketing to Bolt users (or vice-versa) and the data subjects have *not been sufficiently informed*.
*** (c) Bolt is sending third-party marketing to Bolt users (or vice-versa) and the data subjects have *no unconditional right to object*.
* Based on my own research:
** Applicable laws:
*** Instruction No.4 of 2025 ([+LINK+|https://idp.al/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/Guideline-No.04-30.04.2025-Direct-Marketing.pdf]) aligns with the above, other than being silent on the email/SMS carve-out. It is still a binding legal document)
*** E-Commerce Law 2009 ([+LINK+|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1frbgBZ6vmC01hUFmUWK63PKyOzowsKxo/edit]) also aligns with the above. No obvious exceptions for Bolt.
*** Law No.54/2024 ([LINK|https://www.infrastruktura.gov.al/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/Law-no.-54-date-30.06.2024_On-electronic-communications-in-the-Republic-of-Albania.docx]) applies to “_electronic communications networks and the services provided through them_”. Per advice from external advisors, this does not appear to apply to Bolt, except in relation to obtaining consent for cookies ([p.5|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1zq_BbpVgRUDBhI0oz4mgaXNMrRwRoiHd/edit]). If this law did apply, it would require consent for DM.
** Albanian regulator activity re direct marketing violations:
*** The regulator has been laying ‘infrastructure steps’ in 2025 (e.g., publishing Instruction No.4 on DM, and Instruction No.6 on methodology for calculating fines under the 2024 data protection law).
*** There is not a public resource indicating a high volumes of fines. Indeed, the external advisors stated that the interplay has not yet been tested in practice, and so very few cases yet exist which directly show enforcement on this issue.
*** Therefore, overall, the risk is moderate. Difficult to classify it as ‘high’ at this time.
** Commercial agreement division of responsibilities ([LINK|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1s2xGXXAWjVkA_m44Swia8fI8yv8CSwF1/edit]):
*** Per Clause 4.4, the partner is responsible for carrying out “_all necessary marketing activities related to the promotion of the Bolt Platform in the Territory_”.
*** Per Clause 9.2, Bolt may provide marketing support (e.g., templates and tech). The partner must follow marketing guidelines and instructions provided by Bolt.
*** I have also included DM provisions in the DSA.
* Thoughts / Conclusions:
** Current Bolt standard for sending direct marketing is fine for all cases outside of email and SMS.
*** I.e., For those mediums, the legal standard is actually lower than what we adhere to already. As such, adopting our standard approach of: (i) relying on the soft opt-in exception for Bolt marketing; and (ii) relying on opt-in consent for third-party marketing should be fine.
** The position is more ambiguous with email / SMS.
*** On the one hand, the law is extraterritorial in effect, and we are seemingly moving away from it. As such, there is _some_ wiggle room.
*** However, ultimately (per discussions with legal - [LINK|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/D09BUPJRFQ8/p1767372373350039]) we are still aiming for compliance with this extraterritorial law, and we do not have concrete visibility on how precisely these laws interact.
** As such, for email / SMS, we should *aim for opt-in consent to email and SMS marketing (as well as third-party marketing) as a ‘Plan A’*. Other forms can be based on legitimate interest, as needed.
*** NB. No point consulting the regulator on this for now, particularly if the business is unable to implement a solution.
* Action Items:
** Await business confirmation on who is responsible for sending DM / collecting consent ([link|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C09258PDYE9/p1767605626101269]).
*** Presumably this will be the partner.
** Depending on which party is responsible:
*** (A) *Bolt*: Explore opt-in options with the business; if this will not be feasible, then we should fully advise the business of the risks and make sure this is an option in the future.
**** NB. We still do not yet have opt-in anywhere (only coming up in Poland and Georgia). As such, without an objective case, it is foreseeable that the business will not implement an opt-in solution.
*** (B) +*Partner*+: Be diligent in reviewing their consent and marketing practices, and push as needed. Include DSA requirements if needed.
**** NB. We still care as we own the platform, and we are the party that will get any complaints about DM practices.
** Update DM Guidance in tandem.

Hi [~accountid:5f1fbb0eef11df002588080f] We’ve completed a review of the service level agreement (SLA). Please note that the customer provided a PDF and therefore we cannot amend the document. 

Below is an executive summary highlighting the key risks and misalignments. While some provisions are expected in traditional supplier contracts, *they are not appropriate for Bolt Business*. Without significant amendments,{color:#bf2600} the SLA in its current form exposes Bolt to operational, legal, and commercial risk beyond what is warranted for the nature of the relationship{color}.

# *Incorrect contracting entity*: The SLA is with _Bolt Services ZA (Pty) Ltd_, not Bolt Operations OÜ.
# *Nature of the SLA*: The document reflects terms typically used for _traditional goods or physical services vendors_, not for _on-demand digital platforms_ like Bolt Business.
# *Misaligned Risk Allocation*: Several clauses expose Bolt to one-sided liability, penalties, indemnities, and vague service level obligations that do not reflect the operational model of Bolt Business.
# *Overreach*: The SLA assumes Bolt is delivering "products" and services on order with custom deliverables — a significant *mischaracterisation* of how Bolt Business functions.

It is also worth noting that although each McCarthy franchise or branch appears to be contracting individually under separate Bolt Business Special Terms, they all share the same company registration number. This suggests they are operating as a single legal entity, despite functional decentralisation.

* Given this, I suggest a single Data Sharing Agreement be entered into with McCarthy, to apply generally across all locations. cc [~accountid:712020:b2a2738f-c1f1-447c-9b72-29851b5fed3e] 
* In parallel, it would be beneficial to approach McCarthy about *negotiating a corporate-level Special Terms agreement* applicable to the group. This would allow Bolt to set baseline protections and commercial terms consistently, while allowing each branch to continue using their specific operational terms via the short-form Customer Special Terms already in place.
* If we are able to implement our own overarching Special Terms at the group level, they would take precedence over any SLA provisions to the extent of conflict. That structure would provide a much more secure legal and operational foundation for Bolt to consider signing customer SLAs.

I had a look at the section 12 of the MSA on data protection, and here are my thoughts: the section raises a few serious concerns I summarised in the table below.

*MSA Data Sharing Risk Summary*

||#||Topic||Customer MSA Clause Position||Bolt Standard Position||Issue / Contradiction||
|1|*Scope of Personal Data*|Defines Personal Data extremely broadly, including medical, health payment, financial, banking data, physicians, competitors, and any data collected “on GS client’s behalf”|Scope of Shared Personal Data is narrow, specific to Bolt Business context (user phone number, optional name/email, trip/order-level data only)|*Major red flag*: Scope goes far beyond what Bolt processes or intends to process and implicitly pulls Bolt into regulated data categories (health, financial) that are out of scope under Bolt’s standard terms|
|2|*Consent & notice obligations*|Requires vendor to furnish notices and/or obtain prior, informed consents from Data Subjects for collection, use, disclosure, and retention|Each party is responsible for transparency and lawful basis for *its own* processing; Bolt relies on its Privacy Notice.|*Direct contradiction*: Bolt relies on the business customer to provide data to Bolt in course of B2B services.
Where Bolt obtains data independently from users, it can do so based on consent or an alternative lawful basis.|
|3|*Audit rights – scope & method*|Grants GS discretionary audit rights over business processes, books, records, and practices relating to Personal Data|Explicitly excludes on-site audits or inspection rights; only reasonable information sharing and self-audit documentation|*Scope too broad*: Customer clause would override Bolt’s explicit “no on-site audits” position.|
|4|*Definition override language*|Personal Data definition applies “in addition to any other definition in this Agreement”|Bolt relies on carefully layered definitions and annex-based allocation|*Hidden risk*: This wording can silently override the Personal Data Sharing Annex and expand Bolt’s obligations beyond agreed scope|
|5|*Data breach framework*|Broad breach definition tied to audit and compliance exposure|Mutual, symmetric breach notification obligation (48 hours) limited to Shared Personal Data|*Risk amplification*: Combined with audit rights and broad scope, breach exposure is materially higher than Bolt’s standard risk model|

From our discussion on Friday, my understanding is that Bolt’s standard BB T&Cs will also apply. Therefore, my suggestion is to remove section 12 in the MSA & add the following explanatory comment:

{quote} Data protection and data sharing between Bolt and business customers are comprehensively governed by Bolt’s standard Business Terms and Conditions and the applicable Data Sharing terms under Section 4. To avoid duplication and potential conflict with the Bolt Business T&Cs, we strongly insist on removing Clause 12.{quote}

Hey [~accountid:63f5cbdee8216251ae4dc579] - Here’s a high level summary (below). Once you’ve reviewed, let’s arrange a call to talk it through 👍 

_P.S. this information is sensitive and should only be shared in ‘locked down channels’, which is why this ticket exists. We can add additional participants if needed, or I can move this into a restricted access document, no problem._

----

{color:#4c9aff}*Background for anyone not familiar:*{color}

{color:#4c9aff}*(1) Objective:*{color}

* *What?:* 
** Bolt should position itself to credibly demonstrate that drivers operate independently and not for Bolt, subject to other commercial priorities such as market share and GMV.
** Under the Platform Work Directive (PWD), Bolt will be required in EU markets to prove that it is not acting as an employer. Failing to do so will result in Bolt being treated as the legal employer by default. While market level details remain to be confirmed, the underlying framework will be broadly consistent across the EU.
** Member states are required to actively enforce this regime. As a result, Bolt may face scrutiny and enforcement action from authorities even where driver sentiment is positive.
* *Where?:* Priority should be EU markets, followed by other jurisdictions where misclassification risk is material.
* *When?:* For EU markets, implementation should be completed by end of 2026 at the latest. Earlier implementation is strongly preferable. Claims may still be brought in respect of periods prior to 2027 and local authorities are already seeking clarity on Bolt’s operating model.

{color:#4c9aff}*(2) Project Green (PG) recap:*{color}

PG is an ongoing UK initiative aimed at maximising commercial leverage and reducing reclassification risk. Many of its outputs are relevant beyond the UK. Key features:

* *UK agency model relaunch* 
For information only. This element is UK specific and not directly transferable to other markets.
* *‘Substitution / Delegation’* 
For it’s agency model, PG strengthens Bolt’s ability to demonstrate that drivers can
(i) appoint others to perform work on their behalf; and
(ii) work for whomever they choose without Bolt interference.
Previously, this was supported through the Fleet Portal. PG materially improves on that model in two key respects: 
** *Mid order substitution*
Where Driver A and Driver B are online at the same time, Driver A can accept a ride and delegate it to Driver B in real time. This is a significant development, although some issues remain.
** *Account switching*
Drivers can hold multiple profiles and switch between working for themselves or for another person at the click of a button once onboarded. This supports the position that Bolt does not restrict how or for whom drivers work.
* *‘Price bidding’* 
Drivers set their own prices. Not expanded on here to keep things as short as possible.

Additional initiatives have been identified but have not yet been prioritised for development. Further detail to follow (see below).

----

{color:#ff5630}*Questions / Next Steps:*{color}

{color:#ff5630}*(1) What should be extended to new markets*{color}

* As a default, Bolt should aim to deploy both price bidding and Substitution 2.0 in each EU market, subject to local team buy-in and confirmation that there are no local blockers.
** If drivers have no ability to appoint substitutes at all, this could be an instant failure for Bolt.
** Local transport rules or regulator positions may restrict certain features. That said, the fact that these features can be rolled out in the UK should be taken as a positive signal for wider deployment.
** Price bidding has performed well in the UK for both drivers and riders, but this outcome may not translate directly to other markets.
** From my most recent chats with [~accountid:62722e092db308007024a425], both the Netherlands and Switzerland teams appear supportive of deploying these features.
* Other features mentioned below could be extended too.

{color:#ff5630}*(2) Phase 3 extension of Project Green - whats needed (for UK and elsewhere)*{color}

* *UK - development is necessary to help promote substitution uptake:*
** Further development is required to ensure substitution is a genuine and visible part of the Bolt offering rather than a hidden feature.In practice, this requires all of the following.
*** The feature functions reliably. This has been achieved.
*** Bolt actively promotes the feature so drivers are aware of it. Currently blocked.
*** Evidence that substitution is actually used, including mid order substitution. This is the strongest proof point and is currently blocked. We should expect regulators to ask for this.
** To date, the feature has not been promoted because the local team does not yet consider the commercial proposition strong enough to stand behind publicly.
** In particular, the local team wants functionality allowing passengers to favourite fleets or drivers under a trading name. Until this is delivered, progress is limited.
** Key local stakeholders are Ed Riley and Ieva Fowler. I will follow up with Ieva Fowler for the latest consolidated list of requirements (further to the Christmas break).
** Once the necessary developments are made, a similar promotion strategy should be workable in other markets, with execution then sitting with local teams.
* *Other features requiring development time (UK and beyond):* A fuller list will follow after alignment with Ieva Fowler. Based on current understanding, priorities include:
** *Expanded driver preferences*, for example maximum journey duration. The more drivers can specify what work they will not accept, the better.
** *Driver requirements surfaced post matching*, shown on the rider dispatch screen. Examples include no intoxicated passengers or no hot food.
* *Substitution as a global feature*
** Subject to testing, global rollout of substitution should have low or negligible impact on GMV. This makes it one of the strongest available defence features that can be deployed without materially affecting the rider experience.
** FYI any controls currently applied to fleet drivers can also be applied to substitutes, so no material safety concerns should arise.

Hello, [~accountid:5b8d306bfa38ae2c89608b95] and [~accountid:712020:ed417274-8cb0-4891-8fc6-bdf737cb3acb] ! I am back with legal analysis and recommendations related to the certificate of courier bags. I am uploading [the whole recommendations of the external legal from CZ|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1gBPxr86jmvGX5gpJPA-DTYX1BiLzN9jCiGjaskLFITQ/edit?tab=t.0] as well.

+*Summarized conclusion:*+ 

:orange_circle: From a practical POV, *the certificate cannot be considered sufficient proof of compliance with Czech food law requirements on its own, and may only be used as a supporting technical document within a broader compliance framework. Compliance must be demonstrated primarily through a properly implemented HACCP system by delivery partners, supported by operational procedures during transport.*

:green_circle: From a legal POV, t*he fact that the certificate does not contain detailed argumentation regarding contamination prevention does* +*not*+, in itself, *constitute a deficiency from a Czech-law perspective*, provided that contamination risks are properly identified, managed, and documented within the delivery partner’s HACCP system and *adequately addressed in practice.*

*Similarly, the absence of any reference to temperature monitoring in the certificate does not affect its formal validity*{color:#ff5630}*.*{color} However, a lack of actual temperature monitoring in operation would amount to non-compliance with Czech and EU food law requirements, if monitoring is necessary.

:green_circle: In a few words: *As a starting point for assessing the suitability of the box for food transport and its temperature-maintaining properties, the available documentation may be sufficient. Ultimately, however, the legal and practical adequacy of this approach will depend on how rigorously the partners approach their HACCP obligations and to what extent they are prepared to rely on the submitted certificate when assessing and documenting the associated risks.*

(!) If a higher level of legal certainty is required (e.g. for commercial partners), a *further option would be to have the transport box tested and certified by an EU-based or EU-accredited certification authority* applying a recognized and transparent testing methodology. The certificate was issued by a non-EU testing body (China), which further limits its persuasive value in the context of demonstrating compliance with EU and Czech food law requirements.

+*Details*+ 👇 

*_Does this certificate comply with the Czech law if there are any specific regulations related to food transport?_*

* the submitted certificate does not, in itself, demonstrate compliance with Czech law or EU food transport regulations. While Czech and EU legislation does not require a specific certificate for transport boxes as such, compliance must be evidenced by showing that food is transported under controlled conditions that ensure legally required temperatures throughout the entire delivery process. Practically it is addressed through the delivery partner’s HACCP plan, taking into account good practice and the specific nature of the operator’s activities.

*_Is it sufficient from the Czech law perspective that the certificate does not indicate detailed argumentation for Contamination Prevention of the bag?_*

* From a Czech-law perspective, it is not required that the certificate itself contain a detailed assessment of contamination prevention measures applicable to the transport box.
* It must be addressed at the level of the delivery partners, through appropriate organizational and technical measures reflected in the HACCP documentation.

*_Should the certificate explicitly indicate that temperature logging or monitoring devices are in place for consistent temperature checks during transit?_*

* Temperature monitoring itself is a legal requirement arising from Regulation (EC) No 852/2004 and the HACCP framework. Delivery Partners must be able to demonstrate that required temperature conditions are effectively monitored and controlled throughout transport, and that appropriate corrective measures are in place in case of deviations.

Best, 

Jola

This gives us greater scalability, since it’s a replicable solution that can handle high volumes in real time, without manual intervention. It also gives you the flexibility to process and use the data however you like, allowing you to build internal custom reports and make further edits without needing to rely on our support loop.

If you’re open to this approach, we expect to be able to deliver the webhook setup within Q1 2026.

I've reviewed the case and everything is correct on Bolt's end. The preauthorisation was successfully released, and there is no further action required from us.

Please follow the steps in this Knowledge Base article to advise the customer: [https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/kb/articles/internal/7109163016850?country=global&language=en|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/kb/articles/internal/7109163016850?country=global&language=en]

Advise the customer to *check with their bank* to confirm the release of the preauthorisation. Banks handle these releases differently, and while some are immediate, others may process it as a temporary charge that is then refunded. Sometimes, the payment is reversed without the bank sending a reversal notification to the customer, which might lead the user to think that the reversal has not been made.

The reversal can take up to *30 days* to complete, as pending authorisations typically expire after that time on banks end.

Unfortunately, we don't have full visibility into all the parties involved in the payment processing beyond our payment partner. Therefore, we can't track the exact status of the preauthorisation release once it has been sent.

Thank you,

Marten

h3. *Issue description & root cause analysis*

Firstly, this vehicle (frame VIN *3010E0SB000466*) had historically issues with battery insertion, it was very difficult to align the connectors and get the battery in.

When looking at the vehicle logs, we see that the battery hatch was successfully opened, battery was disconnected, but there is no BMS insert event from IOT side and SoC did not change after Klemet seemingly inserted the battery.

We resurrected the bike by powering it through the wake up port, opened the hatch & removed the battery. After removing the battery, we noticed that the connector had been badly damaged, but the battery was 99% charged according to the indicator:

!image-20260106-081747.png|width=321,alt="image-20260106-081747.png"!

Afterwards we tried refitting a new battery but failed to do so again as previously noted, it was almost impossible to align. After further inspection, we noted that the downtube bottom plate welds had interfered with the battery. The welds were very thick and paint had scratched off from interference with the sharp edges from the battery. We modified the plate welds by grinding them down significantly (see picture), after which it was very simple to connect the battery.

!image-20260106-082949.png|width=537,alt="image-20260106-082949.png"!

This matter can now be considered as resolved (/) . The IOT behaved as expected, there was a mechanical issue.

Banks handle these releases differently, and while some are immediate, others may process it as a temporary charge that is then refunded. Sometimes, the payment is reversed without the bank sending a reversal notification to the customer, which might lead the user to think that the reversal has not been made.

The reversal can take up to *30 days* to complete, as pending authorisations typically expire after that time on banks end.

Unfortunately, we don't have full visibility into all the parties involved in the payment processing beyond our payment partner. Therefore, we can't track the exact status of the preauthorisation release once it has been sent.

Thank you,

Marten

Advise the customer to *check with their bank* to confirm the release of the preauthorisation. Banks handle these releases differently, and while some are immediate, others may process it as a temporary charge that is then refunded. Sometimes, the payment is reversed without the bank sending a reversal notification to the customer, which might lead the user to think that the reversal has not been made.

The reversal can take up to *30 days* to complete, as pending authorisations typically expire after that time on banks end.

Unfortunately, we don't have full visibility into all the parties involved in the payment processing beyond our payment partner. Therefore, we can't track the exact status of the preauthorisation release once it has been sent.

Thank you,

Marten

I've reviewed the case and everything is correct on Bolt's end. The preauthorisation was successfully released, and there is no further action required from us.

Advise the customer to *check with their bank* to confirm the release of the preauthorisation. Banks handle these releases differently, and while some are immediate, others may process it as a temporary charge that is then refunded. Sometimes, the payment is reversed without the bank sending a reversal notification to the customer, which might lead the user to think that the reversal has not been made.

The reversal can take up to *30 days* to complete, as pending authorisations typically expire after that time on banks end.

Unfortunately, we don't have full visibility into all the parties involved in the payment processing beyond our payment partner. Therefore, we can't track the exact status of the preauthorisation release once it has been sent.

Thank you,

Marten

We had a sync with [~accountid:712020:b1a3aa39-56a5-492b-9453-5372da990388] yesterday and agreed that instead of creating two new vague subtypes, we can do a very quick analysis on current adjustment use cases and create a bit more granular subtypes → later, these can be used as basis for revamping the adjustments at a larger scale. I reviewed the comments for *delivery_compensation (not vat liable)* and *deduction (not vat liable)* in RO, BG and EE and suggest the following subtypes instead:

Compensations (from bolt → to courier), 

||*Subtype*||*VAT liable?*||*Scenarios*||
|long_waiting_time_compensation|YES|courier waited at courier for too long; used when long waiting time compensation isn’t automatically applied|
|delivery_distance_compensation|YES|issues with delivery address or distance; delivery distance was longer than communicated|
|earnings_correction_compensation|YES|compensation|

Deductions (from courier → to bolt):

||*Subtype*||*VAT liable?*||*Scenarios*||
|order_not_delivered_deduction|YES|Courier mixed up orders and delivered the incorrect order; swapped orders at pickup; any error with delivery causing the order not to be delivered not due to malicious intent|
|earnings_correction_deduction|YES|Any cash corrections (courier received more from eater, didn’t report that) etc; other earnings corrections where earning was applied incorrectly|
|courier_misconduct_deduction|YES|Courier damaged the order; stolen order; courier picked up the order, but requested to re-dispatch.|
|re_dispatch_deduction|YES|Courier requested order to be re-dispatched (e.g. vehicle issue, order didn’t fit into courier bag), but order was marked as completed by error, hence earnings were deducted.|

[~accountid:712020:634c40ac-eff2-4487-aaa9-f38b92a7bf83] When you’re back from vacation, I appreciate your review of the suggested adjustments' VAT liability.

Having these subtypes should reduce the amount of incorrect use of *delivery_compensation (not vat liable)* and *deduction (not vat liable)* to increase vat compliance.

*Summary of key issues raised in the letter:*

h4. *Repeated Suspension of Driver Account*

* *First suspension*: 11–14 November 2025, allegedly due to an issue with the vehicle year on the PHV licence.
** Driver claims this was factually incorrect, as PHV licences do not show vehicle year.
** Account was reinstated after 4 days, implying Bolt accepted the explanation.
** Reinstated the account on 15 November 2025.
* *Second suspension*: From 24 November 2025 onward, due to alleged incorrect vehicle colour.
** Driver provided multiple documents showing the vehicle colour as "Purple", including:
*** DVLA records
*** V5C logbook
*** Current and previous PHV licences
** Bolt is said to have relied instead on MOT-related records, which the driver disputes as unreliable.

h4. 2. *Ongoing Account Suspension*

* As of the letter date (28 December 2025), the account remains suspended for over a month.
* Driver claims the suspension continues despite having provided all necessary evidence.

h4. 3. *Loss of Earnings*

* Driver claims financial losses of:
** £160 for the first suspension (4 days × £40/day)
** £1,400 for the ongoing suspension (35 days × £40/day)
** *Total claimed: £1,560*, plus ongoing daily loss of £40 until reinstatement.

h4. 4. *Claim for Statutory Interest*

* Seeks interest under *s.69 of the County Courts Act 1984* at 8% p.a.
** £12 accrued as of 28 Dec 2025
** Ongoing at £0.34/day

h4. 5. *Procedural Complaints*

* Alleges poor handling by Bolt’s support team and no access provided to a formal complaints process. 

h4. 6. *Demands and Threat of Legal Action*

* Demands one of the following within 14 days:
*# Immediate reinstatement of driver account and full compensation (£1,572+)
*# Full written explanation of the legal basis for refusal and details of the complaints process
* States that if Bolt does not respond satisfactorily, he will issue a County Court claim without further notice.

I've reviewed the case and everything is correct on Bolt's end. The preauthorisation was successfully released, and there is no further action required from us.

Please follow the steps in this Knowledge Base article to advise the customer: [https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/kb/articles/internal/7109163016850?country=global&language=en|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/kb/articles/internal/7109163016850?country=global&language=en]

Advise the customer to *check with their bank* to confirm the release of the preauthorisation. Banks handle these releases differently, and while some are immediate, others may process it as a temporary charge that is then refunded. Sometimes, the payment is reversed without the bank sending a reversal notification to the customer, which might lead the user to think that the reversal has not been made.

The reversal can take up to *30 days* to complete, as pending authorisations typically expire after that time on banks end.

Unfortunately, we don't have full visibility into all the parties involved in the payment processing beyond our payment partner. Therefore, we can't track the exact status of the preauthorisation release once it has been sent.

Thank you,

Marten

Advise the customer to *check with their bank* to confirm the release of the preauthorisation. Marten

Because Bolt holds a dominant position in Lithuania, an obligation preventing fleets or drivers from using co-financed vehicles on competing platforms may be viewed as an exclusivity or non-compete restriction imposed by a dominant undertaking. This triggers competition law risk, even if Bolt is only a shareholder in the JV.

The reclassification risk is secondary here; the primary risk relates to competition law.

Such a condition *may* be imposed, but it must be *carefully structured and objectively justified*, in particular by:

# limiting the restriction strictly to the *Bolt-co-financed portion of vehicle use*;
# ensuring the exclusivity is *time-limited* (e.g. up to *36 months*).

The justification for the restriction would be to ensure that Bolt can obtain a return on its investment when supporting fleets in the purchase or leasing of new vehicles.

*Note:* the higher the share of vehicles tied to Bolt financing, and the longer the duration of exclusivity, the greater the risk of market foreclosure (i.e. competitors’ reduced access to vehicles and reduced competition), and therefore the higher the competition law risk.

Another important point is that forming a JV may trigger *merger control requirements*. In particular, if Bolt acquires a share in a fleet and the relevant thresholds are met, prior approval from the competition authority may be required for the lawful formation of the JV. For this reason, Legal should be involved at an early stage so that a timely risk assessment can be carried out before any commitments are made.

Advise the customer to *check with their bank* to confirm the release of the preauthorisation. Banks handle these releases differently, and while some are immediate, others may process it as a temporary charge that is then refunded. Sometimes, the payment is reversed without the bank sending a reversal notification to the customer, which might lead the user to think that the reversal has not been made.

The reversal can take up to *30 days* to complete, as pending authorisations typically expire after that time on banks end.

Unfortunately, we don't have full visibility into all the parties involved in the payment processing beyond our payment partner. Therefore, we can't track the exact status of the preauthorisation release once it has been sent.

Regarding this topic, I wanted to flag it to you and get your input.

The local ops team raised concerns about a recurring situation: some fleets request changes to the phone number (and sometimes email) linked to an already onboarded courier profile. In reality, this is being used to allow a completely different person - who may not have submitted any documentation or gone through Bolt’s verification process - to operate under that account. In some cases, the person replacing the original courier may even be in Portugal without a valid residence or work permit.

For this reason, the team wants to implement selfie checks in these cases, in order to verify whether or not it’s a case of fraud.

Do you know if any other market is already doing selfie verification in such cases?

Has Central Legal reviewed this in any past context?

From my side, I think this is something we should definitely look into.

Regarding reclassification risks, I don’t think it necessarily increases them if the selfie check is clearly positioned as a security and fraud prevention tool, used only in exceptional cases (e.g. where identity fraud is suspected or where personal data is changed).

Plus, the selfie check does not dictate how, when, or where the courier performs the work - it simply ensures that the person working is the one properly verified and authorized to do so (which is already a baseline requirement).

At the same time, by enforcing that only authorized individuals can access the platform, Bolt is reinforcing the legality and compliance of the model, rather than assuming the role of an employer.

If it’s decided that this is something we can move forward with, I also have some practical questions:

* Should we consider adding a clause to the T&Cs allowing for identity re-verification via selfie or similar methods in specific scenarios?
* If so, should we involve Privacy and clearly define the GDPR basis (e.g. legitimate interest in fraud prevention)?

Would be great to hear if this has come up before and what is your view.

Thanks!

** {{Group Sequential Testing (GST)}} and {{Fixed Horizon}} successfully control FPR at the designed {{alpha}} level of {{5%}}.
** {{Always Valid Inference (Eppo/mSPRT)}} keeps FPR at a lower level for a limited number of peeks (typically {{< 1%}}).
* Sensitivity
** The Status Quo ({{Sequential Fixed}}) demonstrates the highest sensitivity (at the cost of FPR).
** {{GST}} performs similarly to {{Fixed Horizon}}, with a relative sensitivity loss of only {{2-5%}}.
** {{GST}} significantly outperforms {{AVI}} methods, showing a {{100%+}} improvement in sensitivity.

Based on the simulation results and the current infrastructure, *Group Sequential Testing is a clear winner*.

Re this topic, my thoughts are the following:

*Re reclassification risk:*

The key legal concern here is the potential for reclassification of couriers into employees, if the jackets are seen as a reward or benefit provided directly by Bolt in exchange for performance.

However, based on what was described:

* The initiative is routed entirely via the fleet, not directly by Bolt.
* Fleets define and manage the selection based on their own performance criteria.
* Bolt is simply providing material (jackets) in a pass-through manner, with no direct courier communication of incentive or reward.

As long as Bolt is not perceived as evaluating or rewarding individual courier performance, the reclassification risk remains low.

*Re courier communication, my advice would be:*

Ideally the messages shouldn’t be sent to couriers. However, if the team wants to move forward with this, our advice is:

# The message should clearly state that:

* The jackets are distributed by the fleet;
* The criteria are set and applied by the fleet;
* Bolt is not selecting who receives jackets nor evaluating courier performance;
* This is not part of any employment or contractual reward system.

# This should not framed as an “incentive” or “reward” program by Bolt. Instead, it should be presented as a material support provided to fleets, which may choose to distribute it to couriers based on their own internal criteria.

Thank you!

Hi [~accountid:712020:1d5390cd-af56-43c8-9d12-f431b20183ba] Thank you for raising the ticket. 

 I’ve reviewed the assessment summary and considered the scope of a potential FOIA request.

I don’t think it's realistic to ask for Lime’s full offer, or the full offer of any bidder ranked above Bolt. Requests for full competitor bids are almost always refused under FOIA on the basis of commercial confidentiality and protection of trade secrets, particularly in a recent procurement context.

We could, in theory, ask for redacted versions of competitor offers. However, in practice these requests are still very likely to be refused or result in disclosures so heavily redacted that they add little value beyond what we already have in the assessment summary. Also, including this in the wider FOIA increases the risk of a broader refusal or delay across the request as a whole.

I  recommend a narrower FOIA focused on transparency of ranking, scoring and moderation. We already have detailed feedback on our own bid, but we don’t have equivalent visibility of how bidders above us were ranked and how scores were finalised at an overall level.

A more realistic and useful FOIA would therefore ask for:

* the final ranking of all compliant bidders ranked above Bolt.
* the overall weighted scores achieved by bidders ranked above Bolt
* any moderation records or summary notes used to finalise scores across evaluators, in redacted form if needed

This approach is much more likely to succeed as it aligns with procurement transparency principles. 


If you’re happy with that, I can draft an FOIA on this basis for you to review.

* This process just marks order, so there a notification on order page.

** So, it is interesting how the refund was done in this case: was it auto refund, or some CS agent made it manually due to this notification ?

As discussed with [~accountid:631f27278738d3ca32254937] , I could change the date format as in the designs, but it might not work well with all languages.

I have actually asked Chat GPT to understand more specifically which languages it might not work well with and why, and it provided quite comprehensive response (see below).

Given that accessibility is more important and now we use international format, I will close this task with no action (we are currently using what chat GPT suggests is the best practice section).

----

Chat GPT response re: why does this custom format not work in all languages:

Short answer: *it works technically, but it does* *_not_* *make sense culturally in many languages/locales.*

Let’s break it down.

----

h2. What the format means in Moment.js

{{"dddd D MMMM • h:mm A"}} expands to:

* {{dddd}} → full weekday name (e.g., _Monday_)
* {{D}} → day of month (1–31, no leading zero)
* {{MMMM}} → full month name (e.g., _January_)
* {{•}} → literal bullet separator
* {{h:mm}} → *12-hour clock*
* {{A}} → AM / PM

Example (English):

{quote}*Monday 8 January • 3:45 PM*{quote}

Moment *will localize the words* ({{dddd}}, {{MMMM}}, {{A}}) if you change the locale — but *the structure and symbols are not universal*.

----

h2. Where it does _not_ work well

h3. 1. Languages that do *not use AM/PM*

The biggest problem is {{h:mm A}}.

Many locales use *24-hour time exclusively* and either:

* don’t use AM/PM at all, or
* consider it unnatural or confusing

*Affected languages/locales include:*

* Most of *Europe*
** French, German, Spanish, Italian
** Dutch, Swedish, Norwegian, Finnish
** Polish, Czech, Hungarian
* *Russia / Ukraine*
* *China*
* *Japan*
* *Korea*
* *Turkey*
* *Brazil*
* *Indonesia*

In these locales, users expect:

{noformat}15:45
{noformat}

not

{noformat}3:45 PM
{noformat}

Even though Moment _can_ translate {{A}}, the format feels foreign.

----

h3. 2. Languages with different word order for dates

Many languages do *not place the weekday first*, or require grammatical inflection.

Examples:

h4. German

Natural:

{quote}Montag, *8. Januar*{quote}

Your format:

{quote}Montag 8 Januar ❌ (missing case ending){quote}

Correct German requires:

{quote}# *Januar* (with declension){quote}

Moment handles month names, but *not grammatical case changes caused by position*.

Affected languages:

* *German*
* *Russian*
* *Polish*
* *Czech*
* *Lithuanian*
* *Latvian*
* *Ukrainian*

----

h3. 3. Languages that require prepositions or particles

Some languages require words like “on”, “at”, or particles attached to numbers.

h4. French

Natural:

{quote}lundi *8 janvier à* 15:45{quote}

Your format:

{quote}lundi 8 janvier • 3:45 PM ❌{quote}

h4. Spanish

Natural:

{quote}lunes *8 de enero*, 15:45{quote}

Moment won’t insert:

* {{de}}
* {{à}}
* commas vs bullets

Affected:

* French
* Spanish
* Portuguese
* Italian

----

h3. 4. Non-Latin scripts & punctuation expectations

The bullet {{•}} is not universally used or expected.

In:

* Chinese
* Japanese
* Korean

Common separators are:

* 年 / 月 / 日
* commas
* full-width characters

Example (Japanese):

{quote}1月8日（月）15:45{quote}

Your format would look alien even if translated.

----

h2. Summary: Where it works vs doesn’t

h3. Works reasonably well

* English
* (sometimes) informal UI in English-speaking regions

h3. Does *not* work well

* Most European languages
* Slavic languages
* East Asian languages
* Any locale that prefers 24-hour time
* Any language with grammatical date inflections

----

h2. What _should_ be done instead

h3. Best practice (recommended)

Use *locale-aware formats*, not hardcoded ones:

{noformat}moment(date).format('LLLL')
{noformat}

or

{noformat}moment(date).format('lll')
{noformat}

Moment will choose:

* correct order
* correct time format (12h vs 24h)
* correct punctuation
* correct grammar (as much as Moment supports)

----

h3. If you must customize

Branch by locale:

* English → {{"dddd D MMMM • h:mm A"}}
* Others → {{"dddd D MMMM • HH:mm"}} or locale defaults

----

h2. TL;DR

{quote}*No —* {{"dddd D MMMM • h:mm A"}} *is English-centric.*
It technically translates, but culturally breaks in *most non-English languages*, especially those using *24-hour time*, *grammatical cases*, or *different date order*.{quote}

If you want, tell me:

* your target locales, or
* whether this is for UI, marketing, or logs

…and I can suggest the _right_ format for each.

Hi,

Thank you for the research and for sharing the proposed solution.

Unfortunately, at this moment, this approach would not be the best solution for us. From our perspective, it makes the most sense for the payment terms in Workday to follow exactly what is entered in Telema, in the same way they currently do for debit invoices.

This is mainly important in relation to *internal correction invoices*. In these cases, we create both a debit invoice and a corresponding credit note internally, and we intentionally align their due dates in Telema to ensure they are processed and settled together. This helps us avoid situations where the debit invoice is paid automatically before the correction credit note is applied or vice versa. 

If credit notes are always set to immediate payment terms in Workday, AP would need to constantly remember that credit invoices behave differently from debit invoices. This increases the risk of errors and requires additional manual checks. It can also lead to confusion, as the credit correction may be applied earlier while the related debit invoice still has a different payment term.

For these reasons, at this stage we would prefer that the *same payment terms entered in Telema are also applied in Workday for credit notes*, rather than defaulting credit notes to the invoice date (immediate).

Thank you for your understanding, and I’m happy to discuss this further if needed.

Best regards,
Carmen
